Introduction to Digital
Forensics
Md Zannatul Hasan
Head of Cyber Space and New Technology Lab 
IGCI, INTERPOL, Singapore 
• The process of investigating digital devices 
for evidence
• Used in criminal, civil, and corporate 
investigations
• Collecting, preserving, and analyzing digital 
evidence
• Key goal: Identify, recover, and document 
evidence
What is Digital Forensics?
Importance of Digital Forensics
Helps law enforcement 
solve cybercrimes
Identifies cyber threats 
and security breaches
Ensures digital evidence 
integrity in court
Essential for corporate 
and legal investigations
Types of Digital Evidence
Computer Files
Network Logs and 
Internet History
Cloud-stored Information Memory Dumps and 
System Artifacts
Mobile Device Data
Emails and Messaging 
Logs
Legal and Ethical Considerations
▪ Chain of custody in evidence handling is very crucial to 
ensure that evidence is not tampered with. Investigators 
must document every step, from collection to analysis, to 
maintain integrity.
▪ Digital Forensics must comply with Privacy laws such as 
GDPR, HIPAA, etc. Investigators cannot access personal data 
without legal authorization, even if it could be useful in an 
investigation.
▪ Investigators must remain impartial and avoid manipulating 
evidence to fit a narrative.
▪ The ethical principle of proportionality must be applied. 
nvestigators should only collect and analyze data that is 
necessary for the case.
Digital Forensics Process
Identification Collection Preservation
Analysis Documentation Presentation
Tools used in Digital Forensics
Challenges in Digital Forensics
Encryption and Data Protection Mechanisms
Cloud Computing and Remote Storage Challenges
Large Volumes of Digital Evidence
Rapidly evolving technology and cyber threats
Anti-Forensics Techniques
• Cybercrime investigations (fraud, hacking, 
identity theft)
• Corporate security and insider threat 
detection
• Incident response and security breaches
• Intellectual property theft and data leaks
• Terrorism and organized crime 
investigations
Real World Applications 
Digital Evidence and
Crime Scene Handling
Learning Objectives
▪ Define digital evidence and its role in
investigations
▪ Identify types and sources of digital
evidence
▪ Understand how to secure and process a
digital crime scene
▪ Apply legal and ethical practices
▪ Avoid common mistakes during evidence
handling
• Digital evidence is information stored
or transmitted in binary form that may
be relied on in court.
• Supports criminal, civil, and
administrative investigations
• Can reconstruct timelines and reveal
user behavior
• Often requires forensic tools for
extraction and interpretation
Understanding Digital Evidence
Types of Digital Evidence
Computer Files

and Laptops

Wearables

Surveillance Systems

Email Servers
Network Devices
External Storage
(USB, SSDs)
Legal and Ethical Considerations
▪ Chain of custody in evidence handling is very crucial to
ensure that evidence is not tampered with. Investigators
must document every step, from collection to analysis, to
maintain integrity.
▪ Digital Forensics must comply with Privacy laws such as
GDPR, HIPAA, etc. Investigators cannot access personal data
without legal authorization, even if it could be useful in an
investigation.
▪ Investigators must remain impartial and avoid manipulating
evidence to fit a narrative.
▪ The ethical principle of proportionality must be applied.
nvestigators should only collect and analyze data that is
necessary for the case.
First Responder Role
▪ As a first responder, you are the gatekeeper of
digital truth. What you do—or don’t do—in
those first few moments can preserve
evidence that solves a case or destroy it
beyond recovery
▪ Secure the scene and prevent device access
▪ Photograph and document device condition
▪ Record time, people present, and actions taken
▪ Preserve digital state (powered on/off)
Securing the Digital Crime Scene
▪ Disconnect from networks - Remove Ethernet cables
and disable Wi-Fi to prevent remote commands or
data exfiltration.
▪ Prevent remote access or data wiping - Check for
active connections, VPNs, remote desktop sessions, or
device sync settings that could trigger data loss.
▪ Use Faraday bags for mobile devices - Block signals
(Wi-Fi, cellular, Bluetooth) to stop remote wipes,
tracking, or syncs.
▪ Label and isolate all digital equipment - Tag each
device clearly, keep them separate, and maintain
detailed logs for chain of custody.
Scene Documentation
▪ Device make, model, and serial numbers – Record
identifying info for every device, including computers,
phones, and storage media.
▪ Connection ports and peripheral devices – Note
connected accessories (e.g., USBs, keyboards, external
drives), cable positions, and ports in use.
▪ System status (on/off, logged in/logged out) – Capture
current device state with timestamps and screen
photos, if visible.
▪ Any visible signs of tampering – Look for forced
entries, damaged ports, missing components, broken
seals, or foreign devices.
Seizing Devices and Data
▪ Use write blockers for storage devices – Prevent
accidental modification while accessing or imaging
data.
▪ Label and log every device – Assign a unique
identifier and maintain a detailed evidence log.
▪ Preserve media in evidence-grade bags – Use anti-
static, tamper-evident packaging to protect and
secure data storage items.
▪ Avoid turning on suspect systems unless necessary –
Powering on may alter data or trigger destructive
scripts.
Preserving Volatile Data
▪ If device is powered on, capture RAM and active
sessions first – Volatile data is lost once power is cut;
prioritize immediate memory acquisition.
▪ Use trusted tools (Volatility, FTK Imager) – Employ
reliable, forensically sound tools to extract memory
content and preserve integrity.
▪ Document running processes and network
connections – Record live system activity, including
open files, user sessions, active ports, and remote
IPs.
Handling Network Evidence
▪ Collect logs from routers, firewalls, and servers – Retrieve
system and security logs showing traffic patterns, logins,
and access attempts.
▪ Capture network traffic (e.g., with Wireshark) – Use packet
sniffers to record real-time data flows and detect
anomalies.
▪ Map IP addresses, timestamps, and session info – Identify
internal and external communications, user activities, and
potential intrusions.
▪ Export logs in original formats – Preserve original file
structure, timestamps, and metadata for authenticity and
admissibility.
Mobile Evidence Collection
▪ Place phones in airplane mode or Faraday cage – Isolate
the device from any wireless signals to prevent remote
access or data alteration.
▪ Avoid screen interactions – Do not unlock, swipe, or
interact with the device unless you're trained and
authorized.
▪ Use tools like Cellebrite or Magnet AXIOM – Perform
data extraction using forensically sound mobile forensics
platforms.
▪ Record installed apps and network settings – Document
system info, app lists, SIM status, and Wi-Fi or Bluetooth
configurations.
Faraday Cage…
Cloud Evidence Acquisition
▪ Request data through legal channels – Use warrants,
subpoenas, or mutual legal assistance treaties (MLATs) to
gain authorized access.
▪ Work with service providers for access logs – Coordinate
with platforms (e.g., Google, Microsoft, AWS) to retrieve
login data, IP history, and account activity.
▪ Extract files and metadata with timestamps – Download
files, folders, and associated metadata (creation, access,
modification times) without altering content.
▪ Maintain documentation of all access steps – Log
requests, responses, extraction methods, and custody of
cloud-based evidence.
Network Isolation
◼ To preserve the integrity of the stored data, network isolation must 
be employed.
◼ Battery life may become shortened.
◼ Network isolation can be accomplished in several ways 
✓ Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) shielded enclosure or room
✓ Airplane mode / Disabled mode
✓ Operate a phone without a SIM or with a “Forensic SIM” / cloned SIM 
card
✓ Radio Frequency Interference Device Cellular phone jammers (Network 
Interruption Device)
✓ StrongHold Box
✓ Faraday bags & cages
✓ Aluminum foil
✓ Request the service provider to disable the account
◼ NOTE: Battery life will be considerably shorter in a network isolated environment. 
Start with a full battery and set aside enough time to complete the examination. 
For the battery you may need to jump it with a regenerator / reconditioner before 
charging. Make sure you don’t burn-off the lithium.
Device Identification
◼ Form factor
− Bar, Flip, Clamshell, Twister, Spinner, and Slider
◼ Condition of the phone
◼ Make and Model
◼ Hardware Identifier: IMEI, ESN, or MEID
◼ Serial Number
◼ PIN number (Blackberry only)
◼ ICCID of the SIM card
Battery Consideration
◼ Removing battery may cause data loss in devices on volatile memory
◼ Most devices require more than 50% charge before an acquisition 
can take place
◼ Some devices shut themselves off if the battery level drops below a 
certain threshold to protect data stored in volatile memory
◼ Most of the devices will allow a small charge to the device to maintain 
volatile data for a short amount of time (i.e. battery replacement)
Tool Selection
IoT and Surveillance Device Evidence Acquisition
▪ Identify connected IoT and surveillance devices – Look
for smart cameras, speakers, doorbells, thermostats,
and other networked gadgets.
▪ Preserve device configuration and storage – Secure
device settings, onboard storage, and associated cloud
accounts.
▪ Extract logs, footage, and interaction data – Collect
audio/video recordings, motion events, command
history, and device logs.
▪ Document network paths and paired devices – Map
how IoT devices connect to other systems, apps, or
cloud services.
Common Mistakes to Avoid
Failing to Document Actions
Powering on Suspect Devices
Not Isolating Devices from Networks
Using Unverified Tools
Mishandling Chain of Custody
• Incident: Insider theft of intellectual
property from a corporate laptop and
mobile device
• Responder mistake: Failed to isolate
devices; VPN auto-connected
• Result: Remote wipe triggered; critical
data lost
• Key takeaway: Immediate, proper scene
handling is essential to preserve digital
evidence
Case Study
Forensic Tools and
Methodologies
Learning Objectives
▪ Identify different categories of forensic
tools and their primary use cases
▪ Understand imaging, memory capture, and
file recovery methods
▪ Select appropriate methodologies based
on evidence types
▪ Apply forensic workflows to maintain data
integrity and legal admissibility
Digital forensics tools can be grouped based on their function:
• Disk Imaging Tools: FTK Imager, dd – used to create bit-for-bit copies
• Memory Analysis Tools: Volatility – analyze live memory dumps
• Mobile Forensics Tools: Cellebrite, Magnet AXIOM – extract and decode
mobile device data
• Network Forensics Tools: Wireshark – for packet capture and session
analysis
• File System Analysis Tools: Autopsy, Sleuth Kit – analyze file structures and
metadata
Categories of Forensic Tools
Tool Validation and Selection
• Use tools that are forensically sound and
court-admissible
• Verify tool performance and integrity before
use
• Match tools to evidence type and case goals
• Document tool version, configuration, and
results
• Disk imaging is the cornerstone of forensics
• Create exact, bit-for-bit copies of digital media
• Always use write blockers to prevent altering original evidence
• Generate and verify hashes before and after imaging
• Store original and working copies separately. This process ensures that
investigators work from a verified duplicate, leaving the original
untouched for validation and re-examination if needed.
• Tools: FTK Imager, EnCase, Guymager, dd
Disk Imaging Tools
• Live Acquisition is used when the system is on; captures volatile data
like RAM, active sessions, and running malware
• Static Acquisition occurs after the system is powered off; ensures no
data changes during imaging
• Use Belkasoft or Magnet RAM Capture for memory dumps in live
scenarios.
• Tools such as FTK Imager, Guymager, and EnCase are commonly used
for static acquisition.
• Choose the method based on situation and priority of evidence
Live Acquisition vs. Static Acquisition
• Hashing proves your copy is identical to the original
• Use cryptographic hash algorithms such as MD5, SHA-1, or SHA-256
to fingerprint data
• Always document hash values and store securely
• Every step of your process should include a verification phase using
hashes to maintain integrity and ensure admissibility.
Hashing and Data Integrity
File system tools help investigators:
• Reconstruct folder hierarchies
• Recover deleted files
• Examine metadata like last access time, file ownership, and
permissions
Autopsy, Sleuth Kit, and X-Ways Forensics are widely used for NTFS, 
FAT, ext3/ext4, and other file systems. These tools help uncover file 
usage patterns and can reveal attempts to hide, delete, or 
manipulate data.
File System Analysis
• When file systems are damaged or data is deleted, we use data
carving
• Extract file fragments by looking for signature headers (e.g., JPG, PDF)
• No dependency on file allocation tables
• Works well on formatted or damaged drives
• Tools: PhotoRec, Scalpel, Foremost
• Carving is especially useful in recovery of multimedia files and
evidence from reformatted storage.
Data Carving Techniques
• Memory Forensics uncovers malware running only in RAM
• Analyze RAM for active processes, unsaved documents, passwords, 
session keys
• Capture with FTK Imager or Belkasoft RAM Capture tool
• Analyze with Volatility or Rekall, Encase, Magnet Axiom 
• Crucial for live investigations and APT detection. It helps capture the 
dynamic state of a system and expose in-memory threats invisible in 
disk images.

Reporting and Documentation
▪ All forensic work must be clearly documented
▪ Record every tool used, version number, and
process step
▪ Include hashes, screenshots, timelines, and chain of
custody logs
▪ Prepare reports that are clear, professional, and
legally admissible
▪ Your report is your final product—it speaks for your
expertise and process. It should withstand cross-

Best Practices in Tool Use
Always work on Copies, not Originals
Always validate tools before using them in critical cases
Stay updated—tools change frequently
Cross-check results with multiple tools if possible/necessary
Limitations of Forensics Tools
May fail to detect 
encrypted data or 
steganography
May not support newest 
devices or OS versions
Bugs can yield 
false results
User errors or 
unsupported file systems 
can lead to gaps

confidential files. FTK Imager was used
to clone the drive. Autopsy revealed

AXIOM recovered browser evidence
showing files were sent via webmail.
Metadata and timeline reconstruction

Case Study
Definition: Mobile forensics involves recovering digital evidence from mobile 
devices (smartphones, tablets, wearables) using forensically sound methods to 
ensure data integrity.
Significance: Mobile devices are ubiquitous, storing critical evidence like 
communications, locations, and transactions relevant to criminal and civil 
cases.
Scope: Encompasses traditional devices (Android, iOS) and emerging 
technologies like IoT devices and smartwatches.
Example: Extracting text messages to establish a suspect’s communication 
timeline in a fraud investigation.
Overview of Mobile Forensics
• Data Recovery: Retrieve contacts, call logs, messages, photos, videos, and
app data for investigative purposes.
• Evidence Preservation: Ensure data remains unaltered to maintain
admissibility in court.
• Activity Reconstruction: Identify user behavior, including locations visited,
apps used, and communication patterns.
• Investigative Support: Provide actionable insights for criminal cases (e.g.,
cybercrime), corporate investigations (e.g., data leaks), or civil disputes (e.g.,
divorce proceedings).
Objectives of Mobile Forensics
• Device Diversity: Variations in hardware and OS (e.g., Android fragmentation
across Samsung, Xiaomi) complicate tool compatibility.
• Encryption: Modern devices use strong encryption (e.g., iOS Secure Enclave,
Android Full Disk Encryption), hindering data access.
• Rapid Updates: Frequent OS and app updates require forensic tools to adapt
quickly.
• Cloud Integration: Data stored in cloud services (e.g., iCloud, Google Drive)
may be inaccessible without credentials or legal access.
Challenges in Mobile Forensics
• Physical Forensics: Creates a bit-by-bit image of the device’s memory,
including system files and deleted data.
• Logical Forensics: Extracts user-accessible data like contacts, SMS, and app
data without accessing system partitions.
• File System Forensics: Targets specific partitions (e.g., /data on Android) for
deeper analysis, including app databases.
• Cloud Forensics: Focuses on retrieving synced data from cloud services
linked to the device, such as backups or photos.

Email and Social Media 
Forensics
Definition: The process of collecting, preserving, and analyzing digital evidence 
from email and social media platforms using forensically sound methods.
Importance: Email and social media are primary communication channels, 
storing critical evidence for investigations.
Scope: Covers email clients, webmail, social media apps (e.g., Twitter, 
Instagram), and messaging platforms (e.g., WhatsApp).
Example: Recovering a threatening email or a deleted Instagram post to 
support a cybercrime case.
Overview of Email and Social Media Forensics
• Evidence Recovery: Extract emails, posts, direct messages, and media for
investigative purposes.
• Preservation: Ensure data integrity for legal admissibility in court.
• Behavior Analysis: Reconstruct user activities, relationships, and timelines
based on communications.
• Investigative Support: Aid criminal (e.g., fraud), civil (e.g., defamation), or
corporate (e.g., data leaks) cases.
Objectives of Email and Social Media Forensics
• Data Volume: Large quantities of messages, posts, and media require
efficient filtering and analysis.
• Encryption: End-to-end encryption in apps like WhatsApp or Signal
complicates data access.
• Cloud Storage: Data hosted on remote servers (e.g., Gmail, Facebook)
requires legal access or credentials.
• Ephemeral Content: Features like Snapchat’s disappearing messages or
email deletion pose recovery challenges.
Challenges in Email and Social Media Forensics
• Email Forensics: Analyzing email headers, content, attachments, and server
logs.
• Social Media Forensics: Extracting posts, comments, direct messages, and
metadata from platforms.
• Cloud-Based Forensics: Retrieving data from cloud-hosted email (e.g., Gmail)
or social media backups.
• Device-Based Forensics: Extracting app data or cached content from mobile
devices or computers.

title: OC-4 — Human Trafficking: myths, facts and future actions
text:
HUMAN 
TRAFFICKING 
MYTHS, FACTS, AND FUTURE ACTIONS
• Human trafficking often begins with an offer a person cannot 
refuse, like a good job or the chance to get married and create an 
independent life. But instead of what was promised, they find 
themselves trafficked and exploited. 
• The most common forms of human trafficking are commercial 
sexual exploitation, forced labor, forced scamming, and forced 
marriage (including child marriage.)
2
United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) 
as:
“The recruitment, transportation, transfer, 
harbouring or receipt of people through force, fraud 
or deception, with the aim of exploiting them for 
profit.”
3
 Means
• Threats or use of force
• Coercion
• Fraud
• Deception
• Abuse of a position of vulnerability
• Giving payments or benefits
• Abduction
4
Types of Human Trafficking
• Exploitation in the entertainment, sex, 
and hospitality industries
• Domestic work
• Forced marriage
• Forced labor in factories, on construction 
sites, or in the agricultural sector
Without pay?
• Victims are forced to work without 
pay or with an inadequate salary, 
living in fear of violence and often 
in inhumane conditions.
5
WHEN DID HUMAN TRAFFICKING START?
• Human trafficking is not a modern invention. Forced labor, sexual exploitation, and the 
buying and selling of people have existed across cultures and centuries
• The 20th century saw the first serious international efforts to name and prohibit 
trafficking, including the 1949 UN Convention for the Suppression of the Traffic in 
Persons, followed decades later by the landmark Palermo Protocol in 2000
• Today, human trafficking is shaped by globalization, migration, conflict, and digital 
technology. Traffickers recruit online, and people move across borders with ease. 
6
WHERE DOES HUMAN TRAFFICKING OCCUR?
• The Global Slavery Index documents modern slavery and human trafficking in 
every country on earth, including every wealthy Western nation.
• The highest absolute numbers are in Asia and the Pacific. 
• Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand, and Myanmar are among the regions where 
trafficking is most prevalent, driven by poverty, displacement, limited legal 
protections for migrant workers, and demand from both regional and international 
markets.
7
HUMAN TRAFFICKING IN GLOBAL SUPPLY 
CHAINS
•Clothing, electronics, seafood, cocoa, cotton are all 
industries with documented histories of forced and 
trafficked labor at various points in their supply chains.
8
How many people are affected by human trafficking?
According to the Global Slavery Index (Walk Free Foundation, 2023), 
approximately 50 million people worldwide are living in modern slavery, 
which includes human trafficking. Of these, around 27.6 million are in 
forced labour and 6.3 million are in forced commercial sexual 
exploitation. Women and girls make up 71% of all trafficking survivors.
9
Look for clusters of indicators, and trust your instincts.
Signs in a person
• Seems disoriented or confused about their location, the date, or basic facts 
about themselves
• Cannot speak freely — is always accompanied by someone who 
speaks for them or monitors their answers
• Appears coached — gives scripted, rehearsed answers that don’t feel 
natural
• Shows signs of physical abuse, malnourishment, exhaustion, or 
untreated injuries
10
• Has few or no personal possessions — no ID, no phone, no money of their 
own
• Lives and works in the same place, or is transported between locations by 
someone else
• Seems fearful, anxious, or submissive, especially around a particular person
• Is a minor who appears to be engaged in commercial sex or who has an older 
‘boyfriend’ or ‘manager’
• Has tattoos or branding that may indicate ownership — though this is not 
universal
11
Signs in a situation
• Multiple people living in a cramped space with limited freedom of movement
• Someone else holds or controls their identity documents — passport, visa, 
ID
• They are not allowed to speak for themselves in a medical, legal, or official 
setting
• Their story changes or doesn’t match the documentation
• They are unaware of their employer’s address or the terms of their 
employment
12
WHEN SMUGGLING TURNS INTO TRAFFICKING
▪ Sometimes, people start as smuggled migrants but later become trafficking 
victims. 
▪ This happens when they fall into debt bondage, unsafe work, or are 
threatened into doing things they didn’t agree to.
▪ Even if someone consents at first, that doesn’t mean they are safe. 
▪ Once in a foreign place, they may have no choice but to obey due to fear, 
debt, or abuse (Andrees, 2008; Herman, 2006).
CRUEL OFFENDERS VS. HELPLESS VICTIMS
▪ In public debates, human trafficking and smuggling are often shown as a story of evil 
criminals versus powerless victims. 
▪ Events like the Dover lorry deaths (2000) and the Golden Venture shipwreck (1993) shaped 
how people and media view these crimes.
▪ The reality of smuggling is often more complex and involves consent between migrants and 
smugglers, who may be family or friends — not always criminal masterminds.
▪ Migration is not always a solo decision. It’s often supported by migrant networks — groups of 
family and friends who help with information, contacts, and planning . This is known as 
“chain migration” and is driven by both push and pull factors.
WHO ARE THE SMUGGLERS?
• In many cases, smugglers and migrants come from the same background. 
• Studies in the Netherlands show that smugglers often have ties to both home 
and destination countries (Kleemans & van de Bunt, 2003).
• Surprisingly, some smugglers were once smuggled migrants themselves. 
• They use their experience and connections to help others — often for money, 
but not always as masterminds.
HOW SMUGGLING NETWORKS WORK
▪ Smuggling networks are often small and flexible. 
▪ They include people at every stage: origin, transit, and destination. These networks may 
use forged documents, making travel easier — like by airplane.
▪ Without documents, the journey is longer and riskier. 
▪ Migrants rely on local contacts
▪ The process involves more transfers, stops , and coordination. Sometimes a chain of 
loosely connected groups handles the journey from start to finish (Zhang, 2007; Neske 
& Doomernik, 2006).
IS HUMAN SMUGGLING CONTROLLED BY ORGANIZED CRIME?
▪ There is an ongoing debate about the role of organized crime in human smuggling, especially 
in the case of Chinese migrants. 
▪ Studies using law enforcement data show a wider range of organizational types. For example, 
Soudijn (2006) studied 88 Dutch court cases and found that not all smugglers were 
Chinese—about 25% were of other ethnicities.
▪ These smuggling groups take contracts from different sources and work with foreign 
partners. 
▪ While they may not be tightly controlled, they often form stable alliances and have consistent 
group members when the smuggling is running smoothly.
WHO? 
• Countries with high corruption also see more 
trafficking cases. 
• Studies show a strong link between corruption 
and trafficking (Bales, 2005; Studnicka, 2010). 
• In Brazil, 71% of trafficking cases involved 
corrupt officials.
THE TRAFFICKING PROCESS – 3 MAIN STAGES
Trafficking usually follows three stages:
1. Recruitment,
2. Transportation,
3. Exploitation.
Victims are often recruited with false job promises in hotels, cleaning, or entertainment. 
Many knowingly agree to work in prostitution , but often don’t know the real conditions 
(Vocks & Nijboer, 1999).
TRAVEL AND ENTRY INTO DESTINATION COUNTRIES
• Victims often cross borders legally with real documents , using student, tourist, or 
business visas 
• This makes it hard for border officers to identify them as victims.
• In the Netherlands, many trafficked women were found in brothels or window 
prostitution. 
• Some clubs were owned by traffickers, some cooperated, and others simply looked the 
other way.
Bangladesh in the Trafficking Landscape
A Source, Transit, and Destination Country
Source Country → Transit Route → Destination Country
Key Drivers
• Unsafe and irregular migration pathways
• Poverty and widespread unemployment
• Natural disasters and displacement
• Organized criminal networks exploiting vulnerability
Trafficking in Bangladesh occurs through both cross-border movement and internal exploitation, affecting men, women, and children across urban, rural, 
and migration settings. 
Currently, seven major international destinations are active for human trafficking via 
air routes. These include Italy, Serbia/Macedonia, Russia, the USA, Canada, 
Australia, and Cambodia/Laos.
Initially, visas for tourism, education, or employment are obtained. Subsequently, 
the individuals are transported to their final destination via a third country to 
evade direct surveillance by the destination country.
• For those heading to the United States, attempts are made to cross 
the border by traveling from Bangladesh to Brazil first, and then 
through Mexico.
• Individuals are first taken from Bangladesh to a third country—such 
as Nepal—and subsequently sent to Canada.
23
The route to Italy is currently one of the most complex and lengthy ones. 
Traffickers first send migrants from Bangladesh to the Middle East via 
Nepal, India, or Sri Lanka; the journey then proceeds through Egypt, 
Tunisia, or Libya before finally reaching Italy.
On the route to Australia, attempts are made to enter via sea, traveling from 
Bangladesh to Malaysia and subsequently to Indonesia.
The CID has provided information regarding a route to Russia that 
passes through Saudi Arabia.
The CID has also identified two major routes for maritime human 
trafficking. The first route involves transporting individuals from 
Bangladesh to Malaysia, and subsequently to Australia via 
Indonesia.
25
Under the second route, victims are trafficked from Bangladesh into Malaysia via Myanmar and 
Thailand.
Although the law on human trafficking mandates framing charges within 90 working days and 
concluding the trial within 180 working days, trials cannot be completed due to slow 
investigations.
Bangladeshis are most frequently trafficked to India, Malaysia, Thailand, Greece, Italy, Cyprus, 
Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Iraq, Bahrain, and Libya.
The existing law for the prevention and suppression of human trafficking is not being 
enforced due to settlements reached in exchange for money. Yet, the law stipulates 
penalties—including the death penalty, life imprisonment, and a minimum of seven 
years in prison along with a fine of at least Tk 5 lakh—for organized human 
trafficking. Because traffickers evade punishment, they become emboldened and 
subsequently engage in human trafficking again.
He was sold to a cyber scam compound in exchange for money.
Between January and April of this year, 2,408 Bangladeshis traveled to 
Cambodia. However, the relevant authorities do not have information 
regarding how many of them fell victim to human trafficking and were sold in 
that country.
In 2025, more than 15,000 Bangladeshis traveled to Cambodia with clearance 
from the BMET.
28
Bangladesh does not have an embassy in Cambodia. Victims have alleged a lack of cooperation 
from the Cambodian embassy in Bangkok, which handles matters related to the country.
According to the latest Henley & Partners index, holders of Bangladeshi passports can currently 
travel to 36 countries worldwide without a prior visa.
(Electronic visa) or visa-on-arrival can be easily obtained online for a cost of just $30–$36. This 
tourist visa, costing approximately 3,600 Taka, allows for a stay of at least 30 days in 
Cambodia.
The Myanmar military recently conducted an operation in the Shwe Kokko 
area—a region known as an epicenter for human trafficking. As fierce 
clashes erupted between the military and ethnic rebels during the operation, 
thousands of people fled their homes and crossed into Thailand.
30
WHY IT’S HARD TO ESCAPE
Victims often stay due to:
● Emotional ties,
● Fear of LEA
● Lack of better options,
● Shame or stigma.
❑ Free will becomes a blurred concept in trafficking
❑ Many victims believe they chose this life, even when they are controlled and abused
Prevention and Response
• Strengthen child protection systems and early identification of victims 
• Enhance cybercrime monitoring and digital safety education 
• Promote school- and community-based awareness programmes 
• Ensure victim-centred rehabilitation, psychosocial support, and access to justice 
• Improve coordination among law enforcement, social services, NGOs, and child rights organizations 
Media, Culture and Political Commitment
• Utilize television, radio, newspapers, social media, and folk theatre to raise awareness
• Ensure strong political commitment through effective policy implementation
• Promote integrity and accountability, with zero tolerance for corruption
POLICY MEASURES AND INTERVENTIONS
▪ One common way to fight human trafficking is through stricter border control. This means 
building fences, adding security, and targeting physical smuggling routes.
▪ But this strategy has serious limitations. 
▪ Most trafficking for sexual exploitation happens over short distances , and many victims 
travel voluntarily at first — only to face exploitation later.
▪ Strict border control can have dangerous side effects . On the US–Mexico border , many 
migrants now face deadly travel routes.
▪ Research shows that since 2000, over 300 migrant deaths per year are recorded there. Many 
others are likely never found (Guerette, 2007).
HARM REDUCTION STRATEGIES
To reduce the dangers, some proactive strategies were introduced:
● Educational campaigns to warn migrants of risks
● Training and life-saving equipment for border agents
● Search and rescue teams
● Lateral repatriation – returning migrants to safer border areas
These efforts have saved lives, even if the overall death rate hasn’t dropped 
significantly (Guerette, 2007).
ROLE OF TRANSIT COUNTRIES
Transit countries — where migrants pass through — also play a big role in 
stopping trafficking (Perrin, 2010).
They should:
● Check travel documents
● Spot high-risk individuals
● Protect potential victims
● Prosecute traffickers
But this is hard because many victims travel with legal documents , and may not 
even know they're being trafficked yet.
THE SWEDISH MODEL – CRIMINALIZING BUYERS
▪ In Sweden, prostitution is seen as male violence against women. Since 
1999
▪ This aims to change social norms and reduce demand. 
▪ Studies show street prostitution dropped (Statens Offentliga 
Utredningar, 2010). 
▪ However, indoor and online sex work has grown.
THE DUTCH MODEL – LEGALIZATION OF BROTHELS
• In the Netherlands, the ban on brothels was lifted in 2000. Voluntary 
prostitution by adults is legal under strict licensing.
• Fewer undocumented prostitutes
• But problems remain. Many women still work with pimps, and 
trafficking still happens behind legal façades (Daalder, 2007).
FINLAND’S MIXED MODEL
❑ Finland prohibits vulgarity only if the person is trafficked or exploited.
❑ But this raises an issue: How can clients know?
❑ Some clients do report suspicious cases. 
❑ Campaigns like “Appearances Are Deceptive” in the Netherlands encourage 
this (Daalder, 2007). 
❑ Yet, most men don’t take action, even when they suspect exploitation (Farley 
et al., 2009).
BARRIERS TO LAW ENFORCEMENT
o Authorities often focus on business owners , but many exploiters are 
pimps who operate outside the legal system.
o Laws may discourage open abuse, but hidden exploitation continues 
in homes, escort services, or online spaces. 
o Traffickers use manipulation, debt, and emotional control to silence 
victims.
LAW ENFORCEMENT GAPS
▪ In many regions, authorities don’t prioritize trafficking. 
▪ A U.S. survey showed that less than 10% of police agencies identified any 
trafficking cases between 2000–2006 (Farrell et al., 2010).
▪ Also, some countries mix up data on trafficking, smuggling , and illegal 
immigration, making numbers inaccurate or incomparable (Bureau NRM, 
2007).
THE PROBLEM WITH DEFINITIONS
While most countries accept the UN definition of trafficking, they apply it 
differently.
Differences arise in areas like:
● Consent
● Cross-border movement
● Types of exploitation covered
This leads to “the never-ending story of a definition” and unreliable statistics 
(Di Nicola, 2007).
LACK OF EVALUATION IN ANTI-TRAFFICKING 
PROJECTS
• Many anti-trafficking programs lack proper monitoring and 
evaluation.
• For example, in a review of 23 U.S.-funded projects abroad, only 10 
measured performance , and none used strong scientific methods 
(GAO, 2007; van der Laan et al., 2010).
• Without this, it’s hard to know what really works.
NEW INITIATIVES FOR BETTER DATA
Several international projects now aim to standardize trafficking data, including:
● Siamsect Project (EU-funded): Developed a uniform template but was never 
implemented
● IOM-Austria Project (2007): Created 17 guidelines for collecting comparable 
data (Aronowitz, 2009)
● ICMPD (International Centre for Migration Policy Development ) Project: Built 
national databases tailored to each country’s laws and needs (Surtees, 2007)
NEED FOR BETTER RESEARCH
Despite growing attention, solid research is lacking .
 We need to study:
● The impact of immigration policies
● The costs, profits, and networks behind smuggling and trafficking
● Unintended side effects on refugees and migrants
Most discussions are emotional and ideologically driven , especially around sexual 
exploitation (Weitzer, 2010).
EFFECTIVENESS OF INTERVENTIONS
We still know too little about what anti-trafficking policies actually 
work.
Key questions include:
● Which programs protect victims ?
● Which methods prosecute traffickers effectively ?
● Are some policies even harmful or counterproductive ? (Dottridge, 
2007)

title: OC-5 — Drug Trafficking by Organized Crime Syndicates
text:
Drug Trafficking 
By 
Organized Crime 
Syndicates
What Is Drug Trafficking 
Drug trafficking is a global illicit trade involving the cultivation, 
manufacture, distribution and sale of substances which are subject to drug 
prohibition laws (United Nations).
q Key Activities
q Cultivation and Production: Growing or making illegal drugs, such as cocaine, heroin, 
methamphetamine, and fentanyl.
q Transportation and Smuggling: Moving large amounts of illegal substances across 
local, state, or international borders.
q Distribution and Sale: Supplying drugs to wholesale networks, local dealers, or end 
users.
Historical Background
•The earliest “war against drugs” in the US was in response to opium, an analgesic (pain reliever) and central nervous system depressant that can provide relief from stress.
•Before modern medicine, pain relief was a major goal of treatment. 
Opium was widely used to treat Pain; Diarrhea and dysentery; Asthma; 
Fever; Insomnia; Rheumatism and other illnesses
•Opiates were widely available in the U.S. until 1914. Doctors 
commonly prescribed them for various illnesses. It was often available 
without prescription.
•Chinese immigrants helped popularize opium smoking in California.
•Commercial “opium dens” emerged, sometimes becoming associated 
with criminal activity.
Historical Background
Rise of Morphine
•Morphine was developed from opium around the beginning of the 19th century.
•It was much more powerful than opium.
•By the 1850s, morphine products were widely available.
•The introduction of the hypodermic syringe (1856) made injection possible.
•Morphine use increased dramatically during the U.S. Civil War.
After the Civil War
•Widespread morphine use among soldiers contributed to what was called “army 
disease”- Morphine dependence among veterans. 
•Morphine was: Cheap, Easily available, Frequently prescribed and sometimes misused by 
doctors and the public
•Addiction was poorly understood.
Historical Background
The Emergence of Heroin
•Around 1900, diacetylmorphine (heroin) was synthesized.
•It was initially marketed as a safer, non-addictive alternative to morphine.
•Heroin and other opiates remained widely available in the U.S. until 1914.
•After the widespread medical use, misuse also increased rapidly and people were starting to 
understand addiction. This gave rise to government regulations.
British–China trade imbalance: Britain used Indian opium to offset its growing demand for Chinese 
tea. China banned opium, but widespread smuggling and corruption undermined the ban.
•1839: China confiscated and destroyed British opium that enabled the First Opium War (1840–42).
•China was defeated and forced to pay compensation; Hong Kong became a British colony.
•1856–60: The Second Opium War further weakened China and expanded foreign trading privileges.
•The wars demonstrated how drug trade, international commerce, and political power became 
interconnected.
•Impact on the U.S.: The expanding opium trade also contributed to increased opium availability 
among Chinese communities in the United States.
Historical Background
• Chinese workers migrated to the U.S. for mining and railroad work.
• Chinese communities became associated with opium smoking, fueling anti-
Chinese sentiment.
• 1880s: U.S. began restricting opium imports, particularly targeting Chinese 
immigrants.
• 1909: International Opium Commission established.
• 1912: International Opium Convention adopted.
• 1914: Harrison Act introduced federal regulation of opiates and cocaine.
• Drug control shifted from racialized restrictions to formal federal and 
international regulation.
Why Smugglers Do It
1. Huge Profit
Banning a product makes its price skyrocket across borders. Example: Cocaine costs ~$2,000/kg in 
South America, but sells for up to $200,000/kg in Australia due to tight borders.
2. Dodging High Taxes
High government taxes on legal goods create illegal markets. Example: Smuggling untaxed 
cigarettes into Europe yields over $8 million per shipping container with lower jail risks than drugs.
Smugglers and cartels care only about money, not human lives
3. High Demand & Addiction
Addicted buyers will purchase products regardless of cost or law. Example: Cheaply made synthetic 
meth (Yaba) in Myanmar fuels an estimated $60 billion drug market across East Asia.
4. Weak Borders & Corruption
Routine, low-risk business transactions and huge bribes over low securtiy borders.Example: Hard-
to-patrol river borders in Southeast Asia allow gangs to easily move illegal cargo past border posts. 
Narcotics Scenario in the Developing and 
Developed World 
Major Drug-Producing Nations
● Many developing countries serve as production zones for drugs such as:
○ Opium (Afghanistan, Myanmar)
○ Cocaine (Colombia, Peru, Bolivia)
○ Cannabis & Hashish (Morocco, Afghanistan)
○ Methamphetamine (Myanmar, Nigeria)
 Developed World Scenario
 High Demand and Markets: Wealthier nations drive high consumer demand, 
fueling massive profits for international trafficking and synthetic drug 
networks.
 Medicalized Approach: These nations lean more toward public health 
models, providing access to residential rehab, harm reduction, and opioid 
substitution therapy.
 Synthetic Shifts: Markets often focus on prescription opioids, synthetic 
stimulants, and widespread cocaine consumption
 Developing World Scenario
 Production and Transit: Many developing nations serve as 
cultivation hubs (such as opium or coca) or vital trafficking 
corridors, suffering from localized corruption and cartel violence.
 Punitive Measures: Imprisonment remains standard due to a lack 
of healthcare infrastructure and financial resources to fund 
medical treatment programs.
 Stigma: Cultural and moral views often treat substance abuse 
strictly as a personal moral failing rather than a chronic health 
disorder
10
The Global Drug Supply Chain
Drugs are produced in the developing world and consumed in the developed world
Smugglers use:
● Maritime shipping
● Airports
● Border tunnels
● Digital platforms and dark web
The Global Drug Supply Chain
 Raw Materials: Chemical and biological precursors are 
sourced globally to build basic intermediate compounds.
 API Manufacturing: Active pharmaceutical ingredients 
(APIs) are produced, with a high concentration of 
manufacturing centered in countries like China and India.
 Formulation: APIs are converted into finished dosage 
forms like pills, capsules, or liquids at specialized plants.
 Distribution: Logistics networks transport regulated, often 
temperature-controlled products to wholesalers, hospitals, 
and pharmacies
Key Objectives of Drug Syndicates 
§ Profit maximization: Generating immense revenue by controlling the 
production, trafficking, and distribution of illicit substances.
§ Wealth integration: Laundering illicit cash through legitimate businesses, 
real estate, and offshore accounts to blend it into the global financial system.
§ Market expansion: Developing new consumer bases and introducing 
synthetic drugs to create fresh, highly addictive revenue streams.
 Political and Social Objectives
 Systemic corruption: Bribing, intimidating, or blackmailing law 
enforcement, customs officials, politicians, and judges to secure 
operational impunity.
 Territorial control: Establishing governance over specific geographic areas 
(often called "narco-states" or lawless zones) to operate without 
government interference.
 Community co-optation: Subsidizing local infrastructure, healthcare, or 
social services in impoverished areas to buy public loyalty and shield 
leadership from authorities
Major Drug Trade Syndicates Around the World 
Latin America
● Mexican cartels (Sinaloa, Jalisco New Generation) dominate the North American drug 
trade
● Colombian cartels (formerly Medellín, Cali) are key in cocaine production
Major Drug Trade Syndicates Around the World S
Asia
● Golden Triangle syndicates (Myanmar, Laos, Thailand)
○ Produce opium and methamphetamine
○ Run by ethnic militias like the United Wa State Army
● Triads and Yakuza involved in trafficking, money laundering, and distribution in East Asia
Europe
● Albanian mafia, ’Ndrangheta (Italy), and Russian syndicates
○ Control ports, heroin routes, and cocaine markets
○ Have deep political and financial ties
Drug Production in the Middle East & Central 
Asia
This region is a major global producer of opium, not cocaine.
Afghanistan has been the largest opium producer in the world
Heroin made in Afghanistan is trafficked to:
● Nearby countries: Iran, Pakistan, Central Asia
● Other regions: Europe, Russia, China
The drug flows through key smuggling routes to reach these markets.
Countries near Afghanistan have some of the highest opiate use rates:
● Central Asia: ~320,000 users (0.6% of population aged 15–64)
Who Controls the Trade? Middle East & Central 
Asia
1. The Balkan Route:
○ Starts in Afghanistan → Pakistan → Iran → Turkey → Eastern Europe → Western Europe
○ Some traffickers avoid Turkey by going through Romania or Ukraine
2. Northern Route:
○ Passes through Central Asia to Russia and the Baltic States
3. Air Routes:
○ Drugs flown from Pakistan to the UK, Africa, or North America
4. China-India Route:
○ Heroin moves through Pakistan and Central Asia into China and India
Drugs Often Stay in the Region: Middle East & 
Central Asia
Drugs don’t always reach Western markets.
Many are diverted to local markets in:
● Tajikistan
● Kazakhstan
● Kyrgyzstan
This shows the lack of centralized control over the trade. This region produces large 
amounts of cannabis resin (a form of hashish). Cannabis resin is more popular here 
than cannabis herb.
Major cultivation areas:
● Afghanistan
● Morocco
Resin is trafficked internationally, mostly to European markets.
Drug Trafficking Routes in East & Southeast Asia
9 major drug-trafficking routes run through the region.
4 routes originate in Burma, the main source of narcotics.
Key trafficking paths:
● Burma → Laos → Cambodia → Thailand
● Burma → Thailand → Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Brunei
● Burma → India/Bangladesh (less frequent)
● Burma → Yunnan, China → Japan, Taiwan, Philippines
Other routes link:
● Cambodia/Laos → Thailand → Malaysia/South Korea/Taiwan
Some drugs also enter the region from Turkey and Iran
Opium Market in the Region in East & Southeast 
Asia
q Like Central Asia, opium is the main drug produced.
q Most opium stays within the region rather than being exported.
q Burma remains the largest opium grower here.
q Golden Triangle (Burma-Laos-Thailand) is the key production area.
q Production in Burma is often run by ethnic rebel groups like: United Wa State Army, Shan 
State Army-South
q These groups operate with military and political influence in drug zones
Why Afghanistan Matters in Global Drug Trade
For decades, insurgent and terrorist groups used drug profits to fund wars.
This began during the Cold War and continues today.
Opium has been grown for centuries, but Afghanistan’s key role grew after the 1970s.
Why?
● Iran, Pakistan, and Turkey banned opium
● Traffickers turned to Afghan farmers
The Taliban briefly banned opium in 2001, but after they were removed, the trade came back 
strong.
 Massive Decline in Opium Cultivation
 The Taliban’s enforcement of the ban has led to a historic 95% drop in 
opium poppy cultivation compared to pre-ban 2022 levels.
 The Numbers: Total land dedicated to poppy cultivation fell from 232,000 
hectares in 2022 down to just 10,200 hectares. Annual opium production 
plummeted from 6,200 metric tons to roughly 296 tons.
 Regional Shifts: While traditional southwest strongholds have largely 
stopped cultivation, small-scale farming has shifted toward remote, 
mountainous northeastern areas like Badakhshan, sometimes leading to 
violent clashes between local farmers and Taliban eradication teams
 (Ariana News, BBC)
 Methamphetamine: Meth production is booming in 
Afghanistan. It is highly profitable, more covert, more 
resilient to severe regional droughts, and relies on the 
native wild Ephedra plant or cheap chemicals rather than 
vast agricultural fields.
 Global Threat: The UN warns that as Afghan heroin 
stockpiles fully run dry toward the end of 2026, 
international trafficking networks are rapidly switching to 
incredibly potent synthetic opioids like fentanyl and 
nitazenes to fulfill demand, driving up the threat of 
global overdose crises
24
Drug Trafficking Routes Out of Afghanistan
Most opium is exported to:
● Europe, Russia, China
3 major smuggling routes:
1. To Pakistan (160 metric tons in 2009)
2. To Iran (145 metric tons) → then to Europe via Turkey
3. North to Central Asia → 75 metric tons to Russia
Drugs even reach Canada, Australia, and East Asia
Why Burma (Myanmar) Is Important in the Drug 
Trade
Burma is one of the top 3 drug-producing countries in the world.
Joins Venezuela and Bolivia in failing to meet international anti-drug obligations.
Poverty is widespread:
● ⅓ of population lives below the poverty line
● Most people work in agriculture
● Only 34% of people live in cities
Ethnic conflict in areas like Shan, Wa, and Kachin States means the government has little control, 
allowing drug trade to thrive.
Drug Trade History in Burma
Began under British rule—opium was sold widely
Hill tribes in Shan State kept supplying opium even when other regions were 
restricted
After World War II, Chinese Kuomintang forces took over opium trade to fund their 
fight against communists
Today: Burma is a key player in both opium and synthetic drug production
Burma's Methamphetamine Boom
• As opium fell, meth production grew rapidly
• Burma is the main source of meth tablets in the region
• Large-scale "super labs" mostly in Shan State
• Traffickers operate freely in ungoverned areas
• Precursor chemicals now include liquid pharmaceuticals, not just ephedrine
 Production and Scale
 Opium Surge: Myanmar surpassed Afghanistan as the top 
global opium producer following the Taliban's cultivation ban. 
Cultivation reached over 53, 000 hectares.
 Synthetic Drugs: The Golden Triangle region (where Shan 
State meets Laos and Thailand) remains a massive global 
hub for manufacturing synthetic drugs like 
methamphetamine ("ice") and yaba pills.
 Civil Conflict Impact: Ongoing civil war and the breakdown of 
central governance allow armed factions and criminal 
networks to expand narcotics production with little 
interference.
 In recent decades, the country has become a major producer of yaba, a 
synthetic drug distributed in pills easily available throughout the country.
 Rakhine State has now been transformed into one of the major hubs for 
drug transit in the country
 Since the Burmese military (Tatmadaw) seized power under a coup in 
February 2022, drug production in Myanmar has increased
 Shan State, inhabited by Indigenous Shan, Wa, Palaung, Lahu and Akha has 
a long history of being one of the world’s opium (and heroin) repositories
 Traffickers moving drugs either into Bangladesh or Rakhine State are 
sometimes caught by Tatmadaw officials operating border checkpoints.
30
Where the Drugs Go (Trafficking Routes)
Drugs are exported to:
● China, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Oceania (e.g., Australia)
Heroin mostly smuggled overland, especially via the Mekong River
Airports and ports (e.g., Rangoon) are also used
Meth is trafficked to:
● China (Yunnan Province)
● Thailand
Who Controls the Trade?
Armed insurgent groups run the drug business in their territories:
● United Wa State Army
● Shan State Army
● Kachin Independence Army
Ethnic Chinese crime networks are also involved
These groups protect and fund their operations with drug profits
1. The Southern Route: Afghanistan - Pakistan (opium)
2. Andean Region: North America - EU (cocaine)
3. The Balkan Route: Afghanistan - Iran - Turkey - Southeast Europe - 
Western Europe (Heroine)
4. The Northern Route: Afghanistan - Central Asia - Russia - Western 
Europe (Heroine)
Global Drug Trafficking Routes
 The Andean-North American Route: Carries cocaine 
from South America through Central America and Mexico 
into the United States and Canada.
Top Ten
Mexico: A dominant source and primary transit route for smuggling synthetic drugs (like 
fentanyl and methamphetamine) and heroin into North America.
Colombia: One of the world's largest cultivators of coca leaf and producers of cocaine, 
managing vast trafficking networks toward North America and Europe. 
Afghanistan: Historically the world's leading producer of illicit opium and heroin, heavily 
sustaining regional and international trafficking routes. 
Myanmar (Burma): A major center for opium and heroin production in Southeast Asia, 
alongside massive synthetic methamphetamine manufacturing. 
Peru: A top global cultivator of coca and producer of cocaine base, supplying international 
markets via Pacific and overland routes. 
35
Bolivia: A primary cultivator of coca leaf and producer of cocaine, functioning as a key 
regional supply node. 
Ecuador: A major transit hub where cartels move vast quantities of cocaine from neighboring 
Andean nations through coastal ports. 
Honduras: A vital Central American transit corridor for cocaine moving northward toward the 
United States. 
Nigeria: A central West African node and transit point for international trafficking networks 
moving cannabis, heroin, and synthetic narcotics. 
The Netherlands: A primary European entry point for cocaine and a major manufacturing hub 
for synthetic drugs distributed across the continent.
36
Though estimates vary, the illicit 
drug trade generates hundreds of 
billions of dollars per year. 
Criminal groups innovate 
constantly, through boosting 
production, finding new ways to 
chemically conceal their drugs, and 
using technology to conceal 
communications and increase 
distribution. (UNODC, 2025)
International Drug Cartels (recognized by U.S. Department 
of State)
● TdA is a transnational organization that originated in Venezuela with cells in 
Colombia, Peru, and Chile.
● MS-13 is a transnational organization that originated in Los Angeles but 
shifted to Central America as individuals were deported there from the United 
States.
● Cártel de Sinaloa is a transnational organization based in Sinaloa, Mexico. It 
is one of the world’s most powerful drug cartels and is one of the largest 
producers and traffickers of fentanyl and other illicit drugs to the United 
States. 
● CJNG is a transnational organization with a presence in nearly every part of 
Mexico. Notorious for trafficking fentanyl. 
Golden Triangle and Bangladesh
The Golden Triangle: Southeast Asia's Drug Factory
1. What is the Golden Triangle?
● Region where the borders of Myanmar, Laos, and Thailand meet.
● Famous for its massive opium production historically, now shifting toward methamphetamine.
2. Main Drugs Produced
● Opium → Heroin (from poppy cultivation)
● Methamphetamine tablets (known as yaba in South Asia)
● Cannabis resin (in smaller quantities)
Golden Triangle and Bangladesh
Interlinked Regional Drug Dynamics
● The Golden Triangle — covering parts of Myanmar (Burma), Laos, and Thailand — 
is one of the world’s oldest and largest drug-producing regions.
● Bangladesh, though not a major producer, has become a critical transit and 
destination country for narcotics smuggled out of the Golden Triangle.
● Both regions are strategically and geopolitically important in understanding 
Southeast Asia’s narcotics network.
Golden Crescent
● Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran belong to the ‘Golden 
Crescent’ also famous for producing several types of narcotics
● Afghanistan has been untested in smuggling drugs to the 
European countries since 1905
● The land of energy-rich Iran is used as the main route of 
drugs smuggling into Europe from Asia
● Afghanistan (the primary cultivation hub)
Pakistan (major transit zone and refining hub)
Iran (primary transit corridor toward Europe)
Golden Village
● 26-village of Kushtia district in Bangladesh, better known as 
‘Golden Village‘, is also famous for producing cannabis
● Bangladesh lies in between drug producing Golden Triangle 
and Crescent
● Bangladesh are surrounded by Indian and Myanmar hills and 
mountains. Drug peddlers taking the advantages, turned the 
hilly borders as major transit points of smuggling. 
● Using the Bangladesh transit, drug peddlers have been 
smuggling narcotics to northern America, Africa and Europe 
through Dhaka, Chittagong, Cumilla, Khulna and other parts of 
the country.
Golden Wedge
● The Golden Wedge is perhaps the newest route, linking north Bangladesh to the 
Indian states of Himachal Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh
● It expands to encompass Nepal and certain parts of Bhutan
● This strategic location means drug gangs from other countries are also active in 
Bangladesh, including from Sri Lanka and some African countries, and are trying 
to find easy routes to smuggle their product.
● The Golden Wedge is positioned between Asia's two largest illicit drug 
manufacturing zones: the Golden Crescent and the Golden Triangle.
Bangladesh: A Growing Drug Hub
Not a Producer, But a Key Transit Point
● Bordering Myanmar, Bangladesh has become a prime route for smuggling Golden 
Triangle drugs — especially meth (yaba).
● The Cox’s Bazar-Teknaf border, near the Rohingya refugee camps, is the main smuggling 
corridor.
Most Common Drug in Bangladesh
● Yaba (methamphetamine + caffeine tablets)
○ Cheap, addictive, and widespread among youth, workers, and students
● Also trafficked: Heroin, Phensedyl (cough syrup with codeine, from India), cannabis, and 
synthetic drugs
Cross-Border Smuggling Networks
How Drugs Move
● Myanmar → Cox’s Bazar (Bangladesh) by:
○ Boat across the Naf River
○ Hidden on human carriers (mules)
○ Via Rohingya refugee networks (exploited by traffickers)
● From Bangladesh:
○ Yaba moves to Dhaka, Chittagong, and Sylhet
○ Distributed to India and beyond
In Bangladesh 
 Recent nationwide studies by the Department of 
Narcotics Control (DNC) reveal that approximately 
8.2 million people use illegal drugs in Bangladesh 
(nearly 5% of the total population), with the highest 
concentration of users located in the Dhaka division
 Traffickers exploit at least 105 active or vulnerable border points 
across 18 districts to funnel narcotics into the country, 
utilizing land, riverine, and coastal corridors
Smuggling Routes & Entry Points
 The Myanmar Corridor: The southeastern border—including Teknaf, 
Ukhiya, and Saint Martin's Island—remains the primary gateway for 
synthetic stimulants. Traffickers frequently employ Rohingya-linked 
carriers to transport cargo across the border.
 The Indian Corridor: Spanning eastern, western, and northern 
borders (such as Satkhira, Jashore, Cumilla, and Kurigram), these 
routes are heavily utilized for smuggling traditional substances.
 International Transit Hubs: International syndicates utilize Dhaka 
Airport as a transit point to move high-value narcotics (like cocaine) 
from African and South American nations into neighboring India
47
Drug Type Primary Source Market Notes
Yaba & Crystal Meth Myanmar
Accounts for the largest share of 
total drug seizures in Bangladesh. 
Consistently targeted by maritime 
forces.
Cannabis (Weed) India / Local
The most widely consumed 
substance, used by an estimated 
6.1 million individuals.
Phensedyl & Heroin India
Frequently smuggled across 
porous land borders via diverse 
distribution networks.
New Psychoactive Substances 
(NPS) International
Emerging threats include LSD 
(lysergic acid diethylamide), 
MDMA(Methylenedioxymethamp
hetamine), and the unauthorized 
online sale of precursor chemicals.
48
Evolving Methods
 Digital Networks: The illicit trade has heavily shifted to social 
media, encrypted messaging apps, and digital payment systems 
to obscure transactions.
 Vulnerable Carriers: PLOS ONE highlight the growing use of 
women and children under 15 as couriers, often driven by 
socioeconomic coercion or severe poverty.
 Urban Hotspots: Major distribution operations rely on highly 
dense municipal zones, such as Geneva Camp in Dhaka, where 
high population density allows ringleaders to mask their activities.
49
Economic and Social Impact
 Illicit Capital Flight: According to data from the United Nations 
Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), Bangladesh 
loses roughly USD 481 million annually to drug trafficking, 
ranking 5th globally for money laundering tied to the narcotics 
trade.
50
THANK YOU
 https://www.iwgia.org/en/news/myanmar-the-drug-epidemic-in-rakhine-
state?lang=en

title: OC-7 — Counterfeiting
text:
COUNTERFEITING
Presented by:
Md. Rezaul Karim Shohag
Chairperson
Department of Criminology
University of Dhaka
What is Counterfeit Currency?
➢Counterfeit currency is fake or 
imitation money produced 
without legal government 
authorization with the 
intention of deceiving people 
and passing it off as genuine 
legal tender.
➢It is a form of financial fraud 
and economic crime.
➢Forged notes enter circulation 
through illicit networks, 
unsuspecting individuals and 
legitimate commercial 
transactions.
➢Counterfeiting has a long 
history, dating back to the 
earliest forms of coinage.
➢Some of the earliest known 
counterfeit coins were plated 
copies (Fourrées) in Lydian 
civilization.
➢Today's counterfeiters use 
advanced printing techniques 
and high-quality materials to 
create convincing replicas of 
banknotes, make it difficult to 
trace the origin of counterfeit 
currency
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 2
Key Characteristics
✓Illegal Production: Produced without authorization from 
the government or central bank and intended for 
fraudulent use.
✓Intent to Deceive: Designed to imitate the appearance 
and feel of genuine banknotes or coins to mislead 
individuals, businesses and financial institutions.
✓Missing Security Features: Typically lacks or poorly 
replicates security features found in genuine currency, 
such as security threads, watermarks, micro-printing and 
color-shifting inks.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 3
Why Counterfeit Currency is a Problem
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 4
•Financial loss: If you accept a fake banknote, you 
usually lose its entire value because central banks and 
stores do not reimburse you.
•Criminal ties: The illegal trade in fake money often 
funds organized crime, drug trafficking, and money 
laundering.
•Damaged trust: Widespread fakes make people 
hesitant to accept cash, hurting everyday small 
businesses and the economy.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 5
Common Types
•Currency: Producing or passing fake paper money or coins to 
defraud systems and individuals.
•Consumer Goods: Replicating designer clothing, luxury 
watches, handbags, and shoes.
•Electronics & Parts: Manufacturing fake batteries, chargers, or 
critical auto/aviation components.
•Health & Safety Items: Falsifying medicines, cosmetics, food, 
and drinks, which often use harmful or inactive ingredients
Key Risks & Consequences
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 6
•Health and Safety: Substandard or toxic materials in fake 
cosmetics, electronics, and medications can cause severe illness 
or death.
•Economic Loss: Legitimate businesses lose revenue, and 
governments lose billions in tax income. According to reports 
from the The Daily Star, counterfeit items account for a major 
share of local markets, causing billions of dollars in annual 
economic drain.
•Criminal Ties: The counterfeit trade frequently funds 
organized crime, forced labor, and illegal networks.
Counterfeiting Currency
▪ Undermines National Economies: Weakens financial 
institutions and jeopardizes people’s livelihoods.
▪ Fuels the Underground Economy: Can finance the 
activities of organized criminal networks and terrorists.
▪ Reduces the Value of Legitimate Money: Increased 
circulation of unauthorized currency can affect the value 
of genuine money.
▪ Increases Prices: An artificial increase in the money 
supply may contribute to inflation.
▪ Creates Financial Losses: Traders and businesses may 
suffer losses when counterfeit notes are detected and 
confiscated.
▪ Erodes Public Trust: Undermines confidence in the 
currency, financial system and wider economy.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 7
Counterfeit Currency Smuggling Between 
India and Bangladesh
• Major Concern: The India–Bangladesh border has been associated 
with the cross-border smuggling of Fake Indian Currency Notes 
(FICN).
• Cross-Border Route: Counterfeit Indian currency has been reported 
as entering India through Bangladesh, particularly via West Bengal.
• Malda as a Transit Area: Malda, West Bengal has historically been 
identified as an important transit area for FICN smuggling from the 
Bangladesh side into India.
• Smuggling Networks: Criminal networks move counterfeit notes 
across the border and subsequently distribute them to other parts of 
India.
• Bilateral Cooperation: India and Bangladesh have established 
mechanisms, including an MoU and joint cooperation, to prevent 
and counter the production, smuggling and circulation of counterfeit 
currency.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 8
Notable Cases
❑ 2025 — Jhenaidah: BGB arrested a man near the India–
Bangladesh border with ₹5.04 lakh in counterfeit Indian 
currency. According to BGB, he had been living in Bihar and 
allegedly received the fake notes near the border in exchange 
for Tk 60,000, then attempted to re-enter India.
❑ 2023 — Dhaka: Police uncovered a syndicate producing 
counterfeit Indian rupees in Bangladesh, which were allegedly 
used to purchase narcotics and facilitate smuggling 
transactions. The syndicate reportedly distributed counterfeit 
rupees through different border points.
❑2021 — Chattogram: Police investigation identified a 
transnational network in which counterfeit Indian rupees 
allegedly produced in Lahore were transported through Sri 
Lanka and Chattogram, then moved toward India through 
Bangladesh's land routes.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 9
Prevention: Polymer banknotes
❑Polymer banknotes provide greater resistance to 
counterfeiting than traditional paper notes.
Australia pioneered modern long-lasting polymer 
banknotes.
❑1988: Australia introduced a polymer $10 
commemorative note.
❑1996: Australia became the first country with a complete 
circulating series of polymer banknotes.
Polymer technology was subsequently adopted by 
numerous countries, including New Zealand.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 10
Security features and technology
❑Use advanced security features that are difficult to 
reproduce. Examples include:
o 3D security ribbons
o Special printing techniques
o Complex designs and colors
o Distinctive portraits
o Polymer substrates
❑Security features should be periodically upgraded as 
counterfeiting technology evolves.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 11
Maintaining reserve banknote series
❑Countries can maintain reserve or emergency 
banknote series.
❑These notes can be introduced if widespread 
counterfeiting compromises the existing currency.
❑Switzerland historically maintained reserve series of 
Swiss franc banknotes.
❑Reserve designs provided an additional safeguard 
against major counterfeiting threats.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 12
Penalties: Global Perspective
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 13
Country Criminal Penalty
Canada Maximum 14 years' imprisonment
China 3 years to life imprisonment + fine
France Maximum 30 years + €450,000 fine
Germany Maximum 15 years' imprisonment
Hong Kong Maximum 14 years' imprisonment
Italy Maximum 12 years + €3,098 fine
Japan 3 years to life imprisonment
South Korea 2 years to life imprisonment
Macau 2–12 years' imprisonment
Penalties: Global Perspective
Country Criminal Penalty
Netherlands Maximum 9 years + €67,000 fine
Norway Maximum 10 years in serious cases, or a fine
Philippines 6–12 years' imprisonment
Poland 5–25 years' imprisonment
Portugal Bills: 3–12 years; Coins: 240 days–2 years
Singapore Maximum 20 years + fine
Taiwan Minimum 5 years; life imprisonment in extreme 
cases + fines
United Kingdom Maximum 10 years + possible fine
United States Maximum 20 years + possible fine
Zambia Life imprisonment + possible fine
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 14
Counterfeiting of consumer goods 
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 15
Counterfeiting of consumer goods is the unauthorized 
manufacturing, branding, and selling of imitation products that 
mimic genuine items to deceive buyers. 
Key Definition & Distinctions
•Counterfeit Goods: Products that illegally use a registered 
trademark, logo, or brand name to pass as the original item.
•Dupes or Knockoffs: Items that copy the physical design or style of 
a product without using the protected trademark or brand name.
•Pirated Goods: Unauthorized copies of copyrighted material like 
music, movies, or software
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 16
Common Signs of Counterfeit Goods
•Unusually Low Prices: Prices far below market value or 
suspicious, high-pressure discounts.
•Poor Packaging Quality: Spelling mistakes, blurry logos, 
flimsy materials, or inconsistent fonts.
•Missing Details: Lack of serial numbers, batch codes, 
warranty info, or customer support contacts.
•Untrusted Sellers: Purchases from unverified social 
media profiles, random street vendors, or unauthorized 
online storefronts. 
In Bangladesh 
• Top Affected Categories: Personal care and cosmetics: 
Accounts for about 32% of fake goods.
• Electrical and electronic equipment: Accounts for 
~13% (defective wiring drives a high percentage of 
short-circuit fires).
• Clothing and footwear: Accounts for ~12%.
• Food and beverages: Accounts for ~10% (including 
adulterated milk, tea, coffee, edible oil, spices, and 
bottled water).
• Pharmaceuticals: Accounts for ~9%, featuring fake 
antibiotics and diluted critical medicines.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 17
• Many fake goods—bearing copied brand 
names and forged Bangladesh Standards and 
Testing Institution (BSTI) seals or 
holograms—are produced in hidden 
factories around Dhaka, Chattogram, and 
other regional cities. 
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 18
• According to the Bangladesh Cosmetics and 
Toiletries Importers Association, nearly 40
percent of the local market is now controlled by 
counterfeit and adulterated products. Almost no 
sector remains untouched—medicines, food 
and beverages, spices, dairy products, 
cigarettes, cosmetics, fake revenue stamps and 
more are being replicated. (Bangladesh Pratidin)
• The most commonly adulterated items include 
milk, oil, honey, coffee, tea, sauces, chocolate, 
bottled water, soft drinks and baby food.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 19
• According to various studies, including those 
by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics 
(BBS), 80–90 percent of households regularly 
consume milk, tea, coffee and baby food. 
Millions of children depend entirely on infant 
formula.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 20
• Tea, coffee, edible oil, powdered milk, bottled 
water, soft drinks, cosmetics, medicines, 
cigarettes and electrical goods—are being 
sold using fake BSTI seals and copied brand 
identities. 
• Many of these are produced in unauthorized 
factories in Dhaka, Chattogram and other 
cities
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 21
• According to World Health 
Organization data, around 600 million 
people fall ill each year due to 
contaminated food, and approximately 
442,000 die. 
• In Bangladesh, studies suggest that 
millions suffer annually from cancer, 
kidney disease and diabetes linked to 
adulterated food consumption
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 22
Enforcement Gaps:
• Regulatory bodies like the Directorate of National 
Consumer Rights Protection (DNCRP) and BSTI 
regularly run mobile courts and raids (such as 
penalizing dozens of businesses for fake sauces and 
coffee), but enforcement is often reactive rather 
than systemic. 
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 23
Counterfeiting of documents
• Counterfeiting of documents refers to the 
unauthorized reproduction of an official or genuine 
document from scratch to deceive others into 
believing it is authentic. 
• It is a form of document fraud heavily penalized 
under global criminal legal codes
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 24
Common Targets of Document Counterfeiting
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 25
Criminal networks routinely copy high-value documents to 
bypass legal controls or generate financial gain
•Identity & Travel Documents: Passports, driver's licenses, and 
national ID cards to facilitate illegal transit or conceal identities.
•Financial & Security Documents: Checks, stock certificates, 
deeds, and wills used for financial fraud.
•Certificates & Credentials: College diplomas, birth certificates, 
and professional licenses
Legal Implications & Penalties
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 26
Counterfeiting documents is treated as an economic or state crime. 
Penalties depend heavily on the jurisdiction and type of document 
targeted
•Public/Official Documents: Under frameworks like the UNODC 
Criminal Code models, faking official public registers, bills of 
exchange, or wills carries elevated prison sentences (often ranging 
up to 5 years or more).
•Local Statutes (e.g., Bangladesh): According to the Penal Code, 
1860 (Section 476), possessing or counterfeiting authentication 
devices, marks, or seals onto materials to fabricate fake documents is 
punishable by up to seven years of imprisonment and a fine.
Others in Penal Code
