Counterfeiting coins
• Counterfeiting coins is the illegal manufacture, 
alteration, or distribution of imitation currency 
designed to deceive users and pass as genuine 
money
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 28
Common Methods of Coin Counterfeiting
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 29
•Casting (Molded): Pouring molten base metal into wax or plaster molds 
created from real coins, often leaving rough edges, soft details, or casting 
trees.
•Struck Counterfeits: Pressing fake metal blanks between custom-engraved 
steel dies often made using CNC machines and digital scans.
•Plating and Coating: Covering a cheap base metal core (such as copper or 
lead) with a thin layer of gold or silver.
•Clipping and Shaving: Historically shaving or filing small pieces of precious 
metal off the edges of real coins to hoard the excess metal.
•Bi-Metallic Forgery: Painting or mismatching the inner and outer rings of 
modern two-tone coins
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 30
Legal Penalties (Bangladesh Context)
Under The Penal Code, 1860, dealing with counterfeit coins carries 
strict punishments:
•Counterfeiting general coins: Up to 7 years imprisonment and a fine.
•Counterfeiting official Bangladesh coins: Up to 10 years or life 
imprisonment and a fine.
•Making or selling tools for counterfeiting: Ranging from 3 to 10 years 
imprisonment depending on the currency type.
•Importing, exporting, or passing known fake coins: Up to 10 years 
imprisonment
Trademark counterfeiting
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 31
▪ Trademark counterfeiting is the unauthorized production, distribution, or 
sale of goods or packaging that bear a fake trademark identical or virtually
indistinguishable from a validly registered trademark. 
▪ It is a severe, intentional form of trademark infringement designed to trick 
buyers into believing they are purchasing a genuine product.
▪ Difference from Infringement: Ordinary trademark infringement happens 
when similar marks cause consumer confusion about a product's source. 
Counterfeiting involves a direct, fake duplicate of a registered mark placed 
on goods. 
▪ Common Categories: Counterfeit items frequently appear in personal care 
products, clothing, electronics, food, beverages, and pharmaceuticals. 
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 32
Legal Context in Bangladesh
•The Trademarks Act, 2009: Governs trademark rights and 
criminal/civil remedies for illegal copying and misuse in local 
markets. 
•The Penal Code, 1860: Under Section 483, counterfeiting a 
trade mark or property mark carries a punishment of up to two 
years in prison, a fine, or both. 
Counterfeiting of electronics
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 33
Counterfeiting of electronics and parts involves unauthorized components—such as 
integrated circuits, transistors, and capacitors—that are misrepresented in quality, 
origin, or performance to infringe on trademark and intellectual property laws. 
Common Techniques
•Blacktopping / Sanding: Erasing original markings on used or inferior chips and 
applying new, fake logos, date codes, or part numbers. 
•E-Waste Repurposing: Harvesting microchips and components from discarded 
electronics, cleaning them up, and selling them as brand-new.
•Relabeling / Grade Spoofing: Upgrading commercial-grade parts to military-grade 
specifications or relabeling lower-spec components as high-performance or RoHS-
compliant.
•Defective Remanufacturing: Reselling factory-rejected or failed components that 
pass basic visual checks but break down under real-world stress
IN BANGLADESH 
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 34
Economic and Structural Impact
•Market Prevalence: Counterfeit goods account for roughly 39% to 40% of all 
products circulating in the domestic Bangladeshi market.
•Financial Losses: The wider counterfeiting market drains an estimated Tk 
3,170 crore in tax revenues annually and drives over Tk 13,680 crore in 
business losses for legitimate brands.
•The Gray Market Loophole: Many low-quality electrical parts are smuggled 
into Bangladesh from China via unofficial channels. Counterfeiters take these 
components, apply fake local or foreign brand logos (including unauthorized 
Samsung or Nokia labels), and sell them below market price without warranties. 
• Emerging Solutions: To combat this, 
researchers and tech firms are introducing 
supply-chain solutions like TraceChainBD, 
which integrates blockchain and IoT to allow 
buyers to verify components through 
unalterable QR codes
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 35
• Fire Hazards: Fake electrical goods, including 
bulbs, fans, and wires, often fail safety standards. 
The fire service reports that 38% of last year’s fire 
incidents were caused by electrical short circuits 
due to low-quality wiring.
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 36
Counterfeiting of health and safety items
• Counterfeiting of health and safety items involves 
the illegal production, packaging, or labeling of fake 
goods—such as prescription drugs, medical 
devices, hand sanitizers, and personal protective 
equipment—to look genuine for financial gain
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 37
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 38
Common Types of Counterfeited Items
•Medicines and Vaccines: Prescription and over-the-counter 
drugs, cancer therapies, antibiotics, and lifestyle 
medications.
•Medical Devices: Contact lenses, surgical equipment, 
diagnostic tests, and syringes.
•Sanitizing and Hygiene Products: Liquid hand sanitizers, 
surface disinfectants, and toothpaste
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 39
Key Facts and Scale of the Problem
•Economic Losses: Bangladesh loses an estimated $309 million annually from 
counterfeit medicines alone.
•Market Breakdown: Fake personal care items make up 32% of the country's 
counterfeit market, while pharmaceuticals account for 9%. Up to 40% of all 
domestic goods in Bangladesh may be counterfeit due to enforcement gaps.
•Recent Seizures: Law enforcement (such as the Detective Branch) regularly 
raid underground manufacturing hubs, seizing fake syrups, children's liquid
medicines, unlabelled capsule shells, filling machines, and counterfeit hygiene
soaps (such as recent operations in Mohammadpur, Dhaka). 
•Health Risks: Counterfeit drugs and safety items often contain incorrect 
active ingredients, toxic substances, or zero therapeutic value, leading to 
treatment failures, drug resistance, or fatal complications
Consumers' Right Protection Act, 
2009
10 October 2026 shohag_crm@du.ac.bd 40
•Selling or offering expired or fake products/medicines: 
Punishable by up to 1 year in prison, a fine of up to Taka 
50,000, or both (Section 51).
•Market enforcement: The Directorate of National 
Consumer Rights Protection (DNCRP) routinely penalizes 
establishments and seizes fake or unauthorized health

How to Protect Yourself
•Buy from Authorized Sources: Only purchase medications 
and safety supplies from licensed pharmacies, hospitals, or 
direct manufacturers.
•Inspect Packaging: Look for spelling errors, missing batch 
numbers, broken seals, or unusual coloring and consistency.
•Watch for Unexpected Side Effects: Report unusual 
reactions or perceived lack of efficacy to local health 
authorities.

 Concepts of Smuggling

2
WHAT IS SMUGGLING?
▪ Smuggling is the illegal transportation or movement of goods, 
substances, information, or people across a border or into 
restricted places in violation of applicable laws and regulations
▪ Smuggling refers to the purposeful movement of people or 
goods across a border in violation of the relevant legal 
framework (Gallien & Weigand, 2021)
▪ Smuggling is the illegal act of transporting goods or people 
across borders, typically to bypass laws, regulations, or taxes 
(Campbell, 2022)
3
ETYMOLOGY AND HISTORY
▪ The verb “Smuggle” is derived from the German “ smuggeln” or 
Dutch “smokkelen”, meaning “to transport goods illegally”
▪ Both terms are associated with the idea of sneaking or secretly 
transporting something 
▪ Smuggling became a recognized problem in the 13th century, 
following the establishment of a national customs collection 
system in England in 1275 by King Edward I (Gras, 1918)
▪ Medieval smuggling mainly focused on the illegal export of 
highly taxed goods, particularly wool and hides (Williams, 
1959)
4

SMUGGLING

 2. Arms Smuggling

TRAFFICKING VS. 
SMUGGLING
Trafficking Smuggling

financial or other gain.

or goods across borders

movement

8
THEORETICAL EXPLANATION OF 
SMUGGLING
Theory Origin Main Points 
1. Rational Choice 
Theory 
Derek B. Cornish and 
Ronald V. Clarke 
(1986)
 Smuggling is a calculated decision
 Offenders compare profit, risk, 
and punishment
 Smuggling is chosen when 
expected benefits appear greater 
than costs
2. Routine Activity 
Theory 
Lawrence E. Cohen 
and Marcus Felson 
(1979)
 Crime occurs when three 
elements converge: motivated 
offender, suitable target, and lack 
of guardianship
 Weak border surveillance can 
create opportunities for 
smuggling
9
THEORETICAL EXPLANATION OF 
SMUGGLING
Theory Origin Main Points 
3. Push–Pull Theory Everett S. Lee (1966)
 Push factors: poverty, unemployment, 
inequality, and lack of opportunities
 Pull factors: higher profits, demand, 
and better economic opportunities
 Smuggling may result from the 
interaction of these factors
4. Network Theory Mark S. Granovetter 
(1973)
 Smuggling operates through social and 
criminal networks
 Networks connect suppliers, 
transporters, brokers, and buyers
 Trust, relationships, and information 
facilitate illegal activities
10
THEORETICAL EXPLANATION OF 
SMUGGLING
Theory Origin Main Points 
5. State–Crime 
Nexus Approach 
Jean-Francois Bayart, 
Stephen Ellis and 
Béatrice Hibou (1999)
 Examines the relationship between 
state actors and criminal networks.
 State officials may sometimes 
participate in, protect, or benefit from 
illegal activities. 
 Corruption and political connections 
can facilitate smuggling. 
 Weak governance may create 
opportunities for illicit markets. 
11
GOLD SMUGGLING
▪ Illegal movement of gold across national or 
international borders
▪ Avoidance of customs duties, taxes, and 
regulations
▪ Can occur through airports, land borders, 
seaports, and informal routes
▪ Facilitated by criminal networks, 
intermediaries, and corrupt officials
▪ Involves methods such as concealment, 
false documentation, and undeclared 
transportation
▪ Can contribute to money laundering, 
corruption, tax evasion, and organized 
crime
 12
KEY MOTIVATIONS
▪ High international value and easy portability – Gold is valuable, 
compact, and easy to transport
▪ Differences in gold prices and taxation – Price and tax differences 
between countries create opportunities for profit
▪ High import duties – Smugglers avoid customs duties and taxes to 
increase profit margins
▪ Weak border controls – Inadequate monitoring and enforcement 
make illegal movement easier
▪ Demand for undeclared gold – Buyers may seek gold outside 
formal markets to avoid taxes, regulations, or documentation
▪ Money laundering and illicit financial flows – Gold can be used 
to move, conceal, or store proceeds from illegal activities
13
MAJOR WAYS
▪ Airport and Passenger Smuggling – Gold is carried by passengers 
across international borders without proper declaration or 
authorization
▪ Land-Border Smuggling – Gold is moved through land borders, 
often using unauthorized routes or avoiding customs checkpoints
▪ Sea-Route Smuggling – Gold is transported through ships, boats, 
or maritime routes to bypass or reduce customs detection
▪ Concealment in Luggage, Vehicles, or Cargo – Gold is hidden 
inside luggage, vehicles, or commercial cargo to prevent detection 
by authorities
▪ Use of Informal Networks and Intermediaries – Smuggling may 
involve brokers, couriers, traders, and other intermediaries who 
help move gold outside formal legal channels
 14
NOTABLE GOLD-SMUGGLING 
COUNTRIES
Regions Countries 
 South Asia Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka
 Middle East United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen
 Southeast Asia Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia
 Africa Sudan, Ghana, Mali, Burkina Faso, Zimbabwe
 East Africa Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania
 Latin America Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Brazil
 Europe Turkey, Switzerland, Belgium, United Kingdom
15
SUDAN 
▪ One of Africa’s major 
gold-producing countries
▪ Large artisanal and small-scale 
mining (ASM) sector
▪ Gold is smuggled across porous 
borders to neighboring countries
▪ Illicit gold trade provides revenue 
outside formal state channels
▪ Gold revenues have been linked to 
armed groups and conflict 
financing
▪ UAE/Dubai is a major destination 
for Sudanese gold
16
GHANA 
▪ Ghana is one of Africa's largest 
gold producers.
▪ ASM accounts for a substantial 
share of domestic gold 
production.
▪ Gold can be under-declared or 
illegally exported.
▪ Smuggling is facilitated by 
informal traders and 
cross-border networks.
▪ Illicit trade causes loss of 
government taxes and export 
revenue.
▪ Environmental damage is 
associated with illegal mining.
 17
ZIMBABWE 
▪ Gold is an important source of 
Zimbabwe's foreign currency
▪ Significant artisanal and small-scale 
gold mining sector
▪ Gold is illegally exported to avoid 
taxes and official marketing channels
▪ Smuggling networks involve miners, 
intermediaries, dealers, and 
cross-border traders
▪ Dubai/UAE has been an important 
destination for illicit gold
18
DR CONGO
▪ Gold is produced extensively through 
artisanal mining
▪ Eastern DRC has particularly significant 
illicit gold flows
▪ Gold can be smuggled through neighboring 
countries, especially Uganda and Rwanda
▪ Armed groups have been involved in 
controlling some mining areas and trade 
routes
▪ Gold can become a source of conflict 
financing
▪ Weak governance and difficult terrain 
facilitate illicit trade
19
COLOMBIA 
▪ Extensive illegal/unauthorized gold 
mining
▪ Armed groups and criminal 
organizations involved in gold 
extraction and trade
▪ Gold used as a source of illicit 
revenue
▪ Smuggling through neighboring 
countries
▪ Environmental destruction from 
illegal mining
20
PERU 
▪ Major gold producer
▪ Illegal mining is particularly 
serious in the Madre de Dios 
region
▪ Gold can enter formal supply 
chains after illicit extraction
▪ Criminal networks benefit from 
illegal mining
▪ Deforestation and mercury 
pollution are major consequences
21
VENEZUELA 
▪ Illegal gold mining in the Amazon 
region
▪ Gold trafficking linked to 
armed/criminal groups
▪ Smuggling across borders, 
particularly toward Colombia and 
Brazil
▪ Gold can be used for money 
laundering and illicit financial 
flows
▪ Weak state control in remote 
mining regions
22
UNITED ARAB EMIRATES 
▪ Receives substantial quantities of gold 
from African countries
▪ Illicit or undeclared African gold can 
enter the formal trading system
▪ Gold may be routed through 
intermediaries and trading companies
▪ Dubai's role makes the UAE important 
in the global gold supply chain
▪ Stronger traceability and 
responsible-sourcing controls can 
reduce illicit flows
23
INDIA 
▪ India is one of the world's largest 
gold-consuming markets
▪ High demand creates incentives for illegal 
gold imports
▪ Smuggling often exploits differences 
between legal import costs and domestic 
gold prices
▪ Gold can enter through airports, land 
borders, and maritime routes
▪ Organized networks may involve couriers, 
financiers, dealers, and distributors
▪ Smuggling causes customs-duty and tax 
losses
 24
 THAILAND
▪ More important as a transit, trading, 
and destination country than as a 
major gold source
▪ Its borders with Myanmar create 
opportunities for cross-border gold 
trafficking
▪ Bangkok is an important regional 
gold-trading center
▪ Smuggled gold may be associated 
with tax/customs evasion and illicit 
financial flows
▪ Border areas can be vulnerable to 
informal gold-trading networks
25
BANGLADESH 
▪ Primarily a destination and transit 
country, not a major gold-producing 
country
▪ Major source: Middle Eastern countries
▪ Important route: Middle East → 
Bangladesh → India
▪ India–Bangladesh border facilitates 
cross-border movement
▪ Organized networks involve couriers, 
financiers, dealers and intermediaries
▪ Causes customs-duty and tax losses
26
Key Routes and Sources
27
•Main Entry Point: Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka 
is the primary air hub for illegal gold consignments.
•Primary Origin: Investigators note that Dubai remains the main 
source for most smuggled gold, alongside flights from Middle 
Eastern hubs like Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, and Kuwait.
•Transit and Border Routes: The Jashore-Narail highway and 
border areas like Benapole serve as key internal transit routes to 
move smuggled gold toward neighboring countries like India.
BANGLADESH 
▪ Gold smuggled through airports 
and land borders
▪ Major entry point: Hazrat 
Shahjalal International Airport, 
Dhaka
▪ Driven by price differences, import 
duties and gold demand
▪ Facilitates money laundering and 
other financial crimes
▪ Key challenges : border 
surveillance, corruption and 
informal markets
Difficulty in identifying 
organized-crime kingpins
28
GLOBAL GOLD SMUGGLING 
ROUTES
▪ Africa → UAE (Dubai): Gold from Sudan, South Sudan & DR Congo moves 
through regional transit countries such as Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya and 
Egypt to Dubai
▪ UAE/Singapore → Bangladesh → India : Gold enters Bangladesh through 
airports and is moved across the India–Bangladesh border, often destined 
for India
▪ Amazon Basin → International Markets: Illegal gold from Venezuela, Brazil 
& Guyana moves through regional hubs and air/maritime networks toward 
North America and Europe
▪ Key Transit Hubs: Dubai, Dhaka, Cairo, Boa Vista and other regional border 
cities
▪ Overall Pattern: Gold-producing/conflict areas → Transit hubs → 
Refining/trading centers → Major consumer markets 29
KERALA GOLD SMUGGLING 
CASE (2020)
▪ Location: Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, 
India
▪ Seized: Approximately 30 kg of gold
▪ Route: Dubai International Airport, UAE 
→ Thiruvananthapuram Airport
▪ Concealment: Diplomatic baggage
▪ Key actors: Smugglers, intermediaries 
and alleged network members
▪ Motives: High profit, import restrictions 
and duty differences
▪ Issues: Demonstrates how international 
transportation systems and legitimate 
institutions can be used for gold 
smuggling
30
BG-148 GOLD SMUGGLING CASE 
(2026) 
▪ Date: 2 July 2026 
▪ Location: Hazrat Shahjalal International 
Airport (HSIA), Dhaka 
▪ Flight: Biman Bangladesh Airlines BG-148 
▪ Route: Dubai International Airport, UAE → 
Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport 
(DAC), Dhaka, Bangladesh 
▪ Gold seized: 160 gold bars (18.720 kg)
▪ Concealment: Gold was allegedly placed in 
the cargo hold of the aircraft. 
▪ Detection: Authorities acted on 
intelligence from the Directorate General of 
Forces Intelligence (DGFI).
▪ Agencies involved: DGFI, Aviation 
Security (AVSEC), Customs and airlines 
security
▪ Legal action: The seized gold was 
handed over to Customs and a case 
was registered with Bimanbandar 
Police Station
31
DETECTION & PREVENTION
▪ Risk-based customs screening
▪ Passenger and baggage profiling
▪ X-ray and advanced scanning
▪ Intelligence-led investigations
▪ Financial investigation and tracing
▪ Anti-corruption measures
▪ Stronger border surveillance
▪ International intelligence sharing
32
ARMS SMUGGLING
▪ Arms smuggling, also known as 
gunrunning, is the illicit 
cross-border transfer, acquisition, 
or diversion of firearms, 
ammunition, and explosives
▪ The illicit arms trade is estimated 
to be worth 1.7 billion – 3.5 
billion USD annually
▪ The black market of arms 
primarily involves small arms 
and light weapons (SALW) 
because they are mass-produced, 
highly portable, and easily 
concealed
33
ARMS SMUGGLING
▪ The illicit arms trade is unique 
because arms are fundamentally 
used to exercise power, secure 
territory, and challenge national 
security, unlike drugs or human 
smuggling, which are primarily 
driven by economic profit
▪ Arms smuggling poses significant 
challenges to the socio-economic 
and political development of states
▪ It considerably increases the 
potential for violence among a wide 
range of non-state actors, including 
separatists, criminal syndicates, 
terrorists, drug cartels, and pirates
34
KEY DRIVERS OF ARMS 
SMUGGLING
Drivers Explanations 
High Profitability Illicit arms generate substantial profits for criminal 
networks
Conflicts & Political 
Instability Create strong demand for weapons
Weak Border Controls Porous borders facilitate the illegal movement of 
firearms
Corruption Corrupt officials enable trafficking, diversion and 
illegal transactions
Demand from Criminal 
Groups Gangs, cartels and armed groups seek weapons
Weak Law Enforcement Limited capacity to detect, investigate and prosecute 
trafficking
Diversion from Legal 
Markets 
Legally manufactured or imported weapons can enter 
illicit markets 35
INTERNATIONAL LEGAL 
FRAMEWORK
Framework Subject-Matter 
UN Firearms Protocol 
(2001) 
✔ A legally binding international treaty that 
requires States Parties to criminalize illicit 
firearms trafficking, establish firearm 
identification and marking systems, and 
facilitate the tracing and exchange of 
information on firearms
Arms Trade Treaty 
(2013) 
✔ Regulates the international trade in 
conventional arms and prohibits transfers 
where there is a substantial risk that the 
weapons could be used to commit or facilitate 
serious human rights violations
36
The 1999 United Nations Report on Small Arms distinguishes between -
•Small Arms (personal use): pistols, revolvers, rifles, carbines, submachine guns, assault rifles, light machine guns.
•Light Weapons (collective use): heavy machine guns, grenade launchers, portable anti-aircraft and anti-tank guns, 
recoilless rifles, mortars under 100 mm.
•Ammunition and Explosives: integral to both categories.
Authorized vs. Unauthorized Arms Transfers
•Authorized Arms Transfer
• Movement of arms (within or across borders) with state approval under national and international law.
• Includes import, export, transit, and ownership transfers.
• Governed by instruments like the Firearms Protocol and Arms Trade Treaty (ATT).
•Unauthorized (Illicit) Transfer
• Cross-border movement or ownership transfer without legal authorization.
• Examples: unmarked weapons, diversion to illegal end-users, or transfers violating embargoes and treaties.
• Grey areas exist: some government-approved transfers may still breach international law.
Cross-border firearms trafficking method
NATIONAL LEGAL 
FRAMEWORK
Provision Subject-Matter 
Arms Act (1878) 
✔ Prohibits the unauthorized import, export, 
transportation, possession, and dealing in arms and 
ammunition. Violations involving illegal import or export 
can result in life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment 
of at least seven years.
Smuggling of Arms 
Act (1934) 
✔ Empowers the government to take preventive action, 
including declaring notified areas and ordering the 
removal of identified arms smugglers from those areas
✔ Provides penalties for violating government orders, 
including arrest without warrant and imprisonment, 
while allowing prosecution under other applicable laws 
as well
39
TYPES OF SMUGGLED ARMS
▪ Globally: Pistols are the most 
commonly seized firearms
▪ Americas: Pistols account for 
over 50% of intercepted 
firearms
▪ Africa & Asia: Shotguns are
 the most commonly found
▪ Oceania: Rifles are the 
dominant type
▪ Europe: Pistols, rifles, and 
shotguns are seized in relatively 
similar quantities
 40
Methods 
• Diversion from government stockpiles: Criminals exploit inadequate security 
measures or corrupt officials to steal or fraudulently acquire weapons from 
state-held armories and military facilities. 
• "Straw purchasing": An eligible buyer purchases firearms legally from a licensed 
dealer. 
• Illicit manufacturing and conversion: This includes the artisanal production of 
firearms, the illegal reactivation of previously deactivated weapons
• Exploiting online markets: The internet, including social media, online 
marketplaces, and the dark web, is used to advertise and procure weapons, parts, 
and components. 
• Theft from civilian owners or dealers: Firearms are stolen from homes, vehicles, 
or the premises of licensed dealers.
• Exploiting the legal trade: Traffickers use falsified or forged end-user certificates 
and other documentation to deceive suppliers and obtain weapons 
Methods of transportation and concealment
• Freight and maritime shipping: For large-scale trafficking, criminals use cargo ships and 
freight containers. 
• Smaller vessel smuggling: Smaller boats like dhows are used for maritime smuggling, 
often with smaller crews. 
• Postal and courier services: Small quantities of weapons, parts, and ammunition can be 
disassembled and sent through private shipping companies and postal services.
• Road transport: Traffickers hide weapons in vehicles, car's structure or gas tank
• Commercial airlines: smaller arms by concealing them in their checked luggage.
• "Ant trafficking": This involves numerous individuals or small groups each carrying a small 
number of weapons on foot across a border. 
• Professional concealment: sophisticated packaging techniques , such as custom-made 
crates or co-mingling illicit items with heavy, legitimate goods (like timber) 
THREATS OF ARMS 
SMUGGLING
1. War & Armed Conflict 
▪ Smuggled weapons fuel and 
prolong armed conflicts 
▪ Strengthen armed groups and 
undermine state authority 
▪ Contribute to violence, 
displacement and difficulties in 
achieving peace 
▪ Example: In the Sahel, illicit 
firearms have contributed to 
deadly violence and conflict 
around gold-mining areas
 43
THREATS OF ARMS 
SMUGGLING
2. Organized Crime 
▪ Firearms facilitate homicide, 
robbery, kidnapping, extortion 
and trafficking 
▪ Criminal groups use weapons to 
gain power, control territory and 
intimidate communities 
▪ Arms smuggling is closely linked 
to drug trading and other 
transnational crimes
▪ Example: Mexican drug-cartels 
rely on illicit firearms to protect 
operations, fight rival groups and 
maintain territorial control
44
THREATS OF ARMS 
SMUGGLING
3. Terrorism 
▪ Terrorist and violent extremist 
groups obtain weapons through 
illegal arms markets 
▪ Illicit arms enable terrorist attacks 
and armed operations 
▪ Arms can also be smuggled to 
generate revenue and finance 
operations 
▪ Example: Firearms previously 
trafficked through illicit networks 
were used in the 2015 Paris terrorist 
attacks
45
STAGES OF ARMS 
SMUGGLINGStages Descriptions 
1. Sourcing / Acquisition 
Arms are obtained through illicit manufacturing, theft, 
diversion from legal stocks, or illegal purchases
2. Collection and 
Preparation 
Arms and ammunition are gathered and prepared for 
movement through the trafficking network
3. Concealment 
Arms may be hidden within legitimate goods or moved using 
false or misleading documentation
4. Transportation 
Arms are moved through land, air or maritime routes, often 
across multiple jurisdictions
5. Transit / Intermediaries 
Brokers, middlemen or transit networks may facilitate 
movement between the source and destination
6. Border Crossing 
Arms are illegally transferred across national borders, 
sometimes exploiting weak controls or corruption
7. Distribution / Delivery 
Arms reach criminal groups, armed groups or other illicit 
buyers
46
ARMS SMUGGLING: ROUTES & 
METHODS
▪ Major Departure : Northern America, 
Europe & Western Asia
▪ Major Destinations: Central & South 
America and parts of Western Asia
▪ Most Common Route: Land borders 
account for about two-thirds of cases
▪ Sea Shipments: Fewer cases, but often 
involve much larger quantities—around 
5× more arms
▪ Smuggling Methods: Primarily 
concealment, misdeclaration, and 
document fraud 
▪ “Ant" Method: Many individuals transport 
small batches of firearms to evade 
detection
47
BANGLADESH PERSPECTIVE
Aspect Contexts 
Major Sources 
Arms have been reported as entering Bangladesh 
through networks connected to Myanmar and India, 
particularly in border regions.
Border 
Vulnerability 
Bangladesh’s long land and maritime borders create 
challenges for preventing illicit arms movement
Key Areas of 
Concern 
Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar and southeastern border areas 
have appeared in reported arms-smuggling cases
Criminal Networks Arms can be supplied through intermediaries, illicit 
dealers and organized networks to criminal groups
Major Threats Gang violence, organized crime, terrorism, political 
violence and other serious crimes
48
COMBATING ARMS 
SMUGGLING
▪ Criminalize illegal arms trafficking 
under the Firearms Protocol
▪ Strengthen investigations and 
prosecutions of arms-trafficking

Chapter 3: Qualitative 
Research Approaches
Ethnography, Phenomenology, Case studies
Ethnography
Ethnography is a qualitative research method used to study cultures and 
communities by immersing oneself in the participants' natural environment to 
understand their behaviors, beliefs, and practices. 
It involves in-depth observation, interviews, and analysis to provide a rich, detailed 
picture of a social setting from the perspective of those being studied. 
The critical case of Street Corner Society
Street Corner Society: The Social Structure of an Italian Slum is an ethnography written by William Foote Whyte and 
published in 1943
Overt Participant observation : Identity was not hidden
Key informant strategy: Reliance on local leader ‘Doc; for both access and rapport with community 
Long term immersion with community: Roughly four years
Flipside with criticisms;
Direct engagement with illegal activities to gain deeper insight (Fraud of votes, engaged in racketeering)
Doc’s influence on work; rivalry with Chick, his local opponent
Anonymity issues 
Types of ethnography
In overt ethnography, the researcher openly declares their role and intentions to the participants (Overt 
Participation)
In covert ethnography, the researcher does not reveal their identity as a researcher (Covert Participation)
Overt: More ethical, easier communication, but may impact participant behaviour 
Covert: Relatively seen as less ethical, more access for the hidden identity, stressful for the researcher 
Phenomenology 
Phenomenology research is a qualitative approach that explores how individuals 
experience and make sense of phenomena. 
It focuses on understanding the subjective meanings people attach to their lived 
experiences, rather than seeking objective explanations or cause-and-effect 
relationships. 
Researchers delve into the "what it is like" to experience something, aiming to 
capture the richness and depth of individual perspectives. 
Methods of Phenomenology
Interviews
Observations
Personal narratives 
Interview types 
Structured Interviews: 
Such interview use a fixed set of predetermined questions which are asked in a specific order. There is limited flexibility in 
such interviews. 
Semi-Structured Interviews: 
Uses more open-ended core questions. The interviewer can explore unexpected topics and ask follow-up probes while 
keeping the session focused.
Unstructured Interviews: 
Such interviews contain no fixed questions or predetermined order. They begin with a broad opening statement and let the 
respondent guide the organic flow of conversation.
Class exercise
Create 10/12 semi-structured interview questions for your research report 
Case study 
Case study research is an in-depth, qualitative research approach that examines a 
specific real-world phenomenon within its context. 
It involves a detailed analysis of a single case or a small number of cases, often 
using multiple sources of evidence to provide a comprehensive understanding. 
Limitations: Limited generalizability, Potential for researcher bias, 
Time-consuming and resource-intensive, Difficulty in replication
Other tools for use in qualitative research
Focus group discussions (FGDs): When a specific, small group of people discuss on the 
topic of enquiry under the guidance of the researcher (who mainly guides the flow of the 
discussion, without influencing the responses)
Benefits: 
In-depth data (when compared to more rigid surveys)
Time and cost efficiency
Interaction is synergized (participants engage with each other, thereby bringing forth more 
nuances)
Main Disadvantages:
Groups can act in a counter manner preventing shy individuals from sharing 
Dominating individuals could influence what is shared within the group

Cyber Crime and Security (MCCJ 525) Course Objectives
This course explores how a "networked" world has bred new crimes and new responses, and investigates how information and communication technology (ICT) has become a tool, a target, and a place of criminal activity and national security threats, as well as a mechanism of response. This course addresses such questions as how emerging technologies challenge existing laws and criminal procedures; how nation-states regulate criminal conduct across traditional geographic and political boundaries; what reasonable expectations of privacy are in cyberspace; and how control is shifting from traditional mechanisms of law enforcement to new regulatory regimes, including technology.
Course Content
The Phenomena of Cyber Crime and Typology: What is Cyber Crime, Difference between Cyber Crime and Regular Crime, Processes; Content related offenses, Copyright and Trademark related offences, Computer related offences, Combination offences, Indicator, Issues Related to Cyber Crime; Intrusion, Hacking, Unauthorized Access
Theories of Cyber Crime: Classical Criminology, Trait Theories, Social Process Theories, Routine activity theory
Cyber crimes against Persons: Threats and Cyber stalking, Cyber bullying and Harassment, Child Pornography, Child Exploitation, Cyber trafficking Obscenity; Digital Evidence Collection, Electronic Crime Scene Investigation
Anti-Cybercrime Strategies: National and global aspects; Cyber crime and Law, Substantive criminal law, procedural law, International Cooperation and Liability of Internet Providers, Digital security act
Cyber crime and Bangladesh: Information Technology Act, Bangladesh, Crime Detection, Preventive Issues and Strategies, Digital Security Act, Telecommunication Act, Pornography Act
Cyber Security at Person/Organization/ State Level. Legal aspects (Laws, International Cooperation and Liability). The computer as a weapon: using a computer to commit real world crimes.
Hacking, known as CRACKING. Government websites are the hot targets of the hackers due to the press coverage, it receives. Hackers enjoy the media coverage. Grey Hat Hacker, Black Hat Hacker, Script Kiddie, Hacktivist.
Counterfeit E-Commerce: Operating fake online shops that display stolen brand logos and trademarks to sell fake products.
Software Piracy: Distributing cracked or unauthorized copies of proprietary software programs online.
Linking and Framing: Hiding original site boundaries or deep-linking to protected material to bypass paywalls or ads illegally.
Domain Disputes: Resolving trademark clashes through policies like ICANN's UDRP Procedures. Global Treaties: Relying on standards set by the World Intellectual Property Organization to prosecute cross-border digital theft.
Cyberbullying & Harassment: Using electronic media to torment, threaten, or humiliate individuals. Online Grooming: Building deceptive digital connections with minors to facilitate exploitation. Hate Speech & Extremism: Distributing propaganda, inciting violence, or promoting racial and religious hatred online. Non-Consensual Image Sharing: Publishing intimate or private media without authorization (revenge porn).
Phishing messages may appear to be from popular social web sites, auction sites, online payment processors or IT Administrators are commonly used to lure the unsuspecting public. Phishing is typically carried out by e-mail or instant messaging, and it often directs users to enter details at a fake website whose look and feel are almost identical to the legitimate one. Even when using server authentication, it may require tremendous skill to detect that the website is fake.
Pharming: Sending users to fake websites by altering DNS settings or code behind the scenes. Mobile and Alternative Phishing. Smishing: Phishing sent through short text messages (SMS) on mobile phones. Vishing: Voice phishing that uses phone calls or synthetic voicemails to steal info. Quishing: Placing malicious QR codes on flyers or in emails that lead to fake login pages. Angler Phishing: Scammers hiding on social media by acting as official customer support.
Solution: Don't configure your system or applications with unknown proxy server settings. Don't click unknown links in trustless websites. Use a good Firewall software available in the market. Don't download unknown files from strange users over the internet. Aware people about phishing and warn about suspicious websites. And strictly use trusted services in internet and application field of your computing.
Malware is a general term used by computer professionals to mean a variety of forms of hostile, intrusive, or annoying software or program code. The term "computer virus" is sometimes used as a catch-all phrase to include all types of malware, including true viruses.
Password cracking is used to recover a forgotten password (though installing an entirely new password is less of a security risk, but involves system administration privileges), to gain unauthorized access to a system, or as a preventive measure by system administrators to check for easily crackable passwords. On a file-by file basis, password cracking is utilized to gain access to digital evidence for which a judge has allowed access but the particular file's access is restricted.
Social engineering is manipulating people into performing actions or divulging confidential information. While similar to a confidence trick or simple fraud, the term typically applies to trickery or deception for the purpose of information gathering, fraud, or computer system access; in most cases the attacker never comes face-to-face with the victim.
Spyware collects personal information, such as Internet surfing habits and sites that have been visited, but can also interfere with user control of the computer in other ways, such as installing additional software and redirecting Web browser activity. Spyware is known to change computer settings, resulting in slow connection speeds, different home pages, and/or loss of Internet or functionality of other programs. In an attempt to increase the understanding of spyware, a more formal classification of its included software types is captured under the term privacy-invasive software.
Although the means to carry out, motives for, and targets of a DoS attack may vary, it generally consists of the concerted efforts of a person or people to prevent an Internet site or service from functioning efficiently or at all, temporarily or indefinitely. Perpetrators of DoS attacks typically target sites or services hosted on high-profile web servers such as banks, credit card payment gateways, and even root name servers.
When we address Cyber Security we're talking about technology infrastructure, applications, data and human interaction. These elements are no longer limited to "wired" net, they now also encompass all forms of converged IP-based communications.
It's War – In fact it is already becoming the next Cold War. Cyber operations are also becoming increasing integrated into active conflicts. To date, it only seems as though the problem is getting worse and Cyber adversaries have a cost advantage that puts defenders at a permanent disadvantage.
There is no single solution or even a single family of solutions that can provide a comprehensive approach to the problem space. A Fresh Perspective – Is what's needed. We can either react to ever-growing complexity and disruption by adding more layers of complication ourselves or we can manage the patterns.
As soon as we consider that conventional operations that rely on IT capability are Cyber Operations then Cyber can become both Kinetic and Non-Kinetic in nature. Cyber Attacks can be real-time events or time-delayed events. They can originate from anywhere or be triggered from anywhere and originate from within our perimeters. They occur in multi-dimension Cyberspace as well as in conventional warfare frames of reference.
Cyber Security isn't something that will or even can go away. As long as our infrastructure remains networked and interdependent Cyber Security will remain critical. Infrastructure Management – Both security architecture and all other architectures. Cyber Operations – Active Defense and Offense. Cyber Integration – Putting it all together. It's Part of a Larger Lifecycle – Viewing threats outside of either the attack lifecycle or the defense solution lifecycle will provide an incomplete view. It's both Strategic & Tactical – And it must be linked.
The key to managing threats is understanding them – the key to understanding them is to find a way to map them against specific behaviors or events. The activities which help provide this definition and mapping represents the core of Threat Management.
Authenticity - Authenticity is necessary to ensure that the users or objects (like documents) are genuine (they have not been forged or fabricated). Availability - Availability means that the information, the computing systems used to process the information, and the security controls used to protect the information are all available and functioning correctly when the information is needed. Non-Repudiation - When one party of a transaction cannot deny having received a transaction nor can the other party deny having sent a transaction.
Information Assurance (IA) represents a set of guidelines for managing security related activities and systems. Originally it was developed in the context of individual systems and smaller networks. Adding "Cyber" scope extends but doesn't replace IA.
An attacker only needs to understand a portion of the technical architecture to compromise it. The Defenders must understand the entire infrastructure to defend it as well as understanding the organizations which manage them and understanding the nature of both internal and external attackers. Becoming an expert in all aspects of IT and Operational Security is quite simply – overwhelming.
As the name implies, NETOPS involves network security but also encompasses aspects of IA, system level security and infrastructure management. The current weakness associated with NETOPS is its focus on perimeter security in limited contexts. Cyber Operations in contrast encompasses all elements in fielded solutions as well as the entire solution lifecycle.
Cyber Integration is a relatively new discipline in that it directly responds to the recent mandate that Cyber Security solutions support both enterprise and multiple domain level scale. Cyber Integration is where the majority of new & intelligent security capabilities will arise from.
What is Cyber Defence? The strategy and technology used to protect networks, data, and critical infrastructure from cyber attacks. Continuous Monitoring: Watching network traffic in real time for strange behavior. Threat Hunting: Searching actively for hidden malware or intruders before they strike. Incident Response: Acting fast to isolate and fix compromised systems. National Collaboration: Governments and private industries sharing threat data to secure national assets.
Types of cyber-attacks: Phishing (whale phishing, spear phishing, pharming), SQL injection, man-in-the-middle attack (session hijacking, IP spoofing, replay), cross-site scripting (XSS), AI-powered attacks, distributed denial of service attack (DDoS), password attack (brute force, guessing, dictionary attack), eavesdropping attack, drive-by attack, ransomware attack.
These steps can help protect you from cyber criminals. Follow cybersecurity best practices and guidelines. Use digital and physical security methods. Keep your software updated. Become cyber aware through self-education or training. Actively manage your social media settings. Talk to your children about the threats. Constantly change your passwords.
Use proper security tools. A good Anti-Virus Software and Firewall Software are better to protect your computer. If you smell any suspicious activity on your system then isolate it from external media or storage to prevent spreading. Contact a technical expert if you are a Entry-Level User. Also scan suspicious external media before access the files on it. Compression or encryption will keep files from virus.
If you face these incidents then immediately cancel all account traffic and transaction. Also cancel your Debit or Credit card temporarily. Don't be panic and move with expert's advice. Aware all others about it and its characteristics and possibilities of such situation.
Maintain backup, check security settings, stay anonymous - choose a genderless screen name, never give your full name or address to strangers, learn to deal with hostile situations quickly, save offending messages, learn more about Internet privacy.
